articles.title: Florida executes man in connection to Hog Trail Murders
articles.summary:
The execution of Daniel Owen Conahan Jr makes him the state’s 15th person executed this year

A Florida man was executed by lethal injection on Thursday after being convicted of one of a…

blocks.text: A Florida man was executed by lethal injection on Thursday after being convicted of one of a series of suspected killings that became known as the Hog Trail Murders in the 1990s.

Daniel Owen Conahan Jr, 72, was sentenced to death for the 1996 kidnapping and strangling of Richard Allen Montgomery. Authorities found Montgomery’s mutilated body in a wooded south-west Florida area where the remains of at least six people have been found over a three-year span.
Conahan died at 6.12pm ET, state officials said.

Florida has carried out more than half of the 24 total executions in the US this year, under Ron DeSantis, the Republican governor who leaves office in January. Conahan Jr is the 15th person executed in the state this year.
Under DeSantis, Florida carried out 19 executions in 2025, setting a state record since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976.

Conahan was arrested in July 1996 after local and state law enforcement officials spent more than two years investigating a series of homicides in which mutilated and decomposing bodies were discovered in a wooded area of Charlotte county, north of Fort Myers.

The deaths eventually were categorized as the Hog Trail Murders because of the swampy, wooded locations where the bodies were found. The case has been featured many times over the past three decades on true-crime media content.

Conahan, who maintained his innocence, was previously identified by authorities as a person of interest in the other deaths, but he was never charged. He argued that the evidence against him was circumstantial.

The first body was found by hunters in February 1994, followed by at least five more bodies over the next three years. Most of the remains were severely decomposed, but investigators believed Montgomery had been dead for less than a day when he was found.
Investigators eventually determined that the killer was targeting men who were unhoused.

Detectives started looking into Conahan in 1996 after a man in prison for stealing Conahan’s car claimed that Conahan had lured him to a remote area and offered to pay him to pose for nude photos. The man said he drove off in the car after seeing a knife.
Conahan waived his right to a jury trial and was convicted by a judge of murder and kidnapping in August 1999.
The Florida supreme court last week denied Conahan’s final appeals, including one requesting additional testing on DNA collected from the victim.

The petition said he has been requesting DNA testing since March 2025 of evidence collected at the scene and from Montgomery’s body to “conclusively establish that he is not responsible for the death”.
Within 24 hours, the court ruled that proving Montgomery had DNA on his body from someone other than Conahan would not exonerate him.
The US supreme court on Thursday denied his final appeal.

articles.title: Generic acetaminophen pills recalled due to possible 'foreign material' contamination
articles.summary: An over-the-counter pain reliever is being recalled due to the possible presence of "foreign material" that could harm the digestive system.

image.caption: Teva Canada Limited is recalling one lot of the non-prescription drug Novo-Gesic Forte 500 mg. (Health Canada)

blocks.text: Canada·New
An over-the-counter pain reliever is being recalled due to the possible presence of "foreign material" that could harm the digestive system.
Teva Canada recalls over-the-counter Novo-Gesic Forte tablets
Teva Canada is recalling a lot of 500-milligram Nov-Gesic Forte acetaminophen "due to the potential presence of phenolic resin or epoxy," according to a Thursday news release from Health Canada.
Health Canada says the pills from Lot No. 100083040, with the expiration date of Jan. 31, 2029, were supplied to pharmacies in 1,000-count bottles and dispensed to patients in smaller quantities.

"Immediately stop using the affected product and return it to your local pharmacy for replacement and proper disposal," the release states. "If you are unsure whether your product is recalled, check with your pharmacy."

The agency says anyone who has used the affected product and has concerns about their health should contact their health-care practitioner, and should report any product-related side effects or complaints to Health Canada.
Customers can also contact Teva Canada Customer Care by calling 1-800-268-4129 or emailing customer.service@tevacanada.com.

articles.title: Cesafi season 26: UC goes 2-0 with win over USC
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — The University of Cebu (UC) Webmasters turned a highly anticipated marquee matchup into a one-sided affair, steamrolling the University of San Carlos (USC) Warriors, 81-63,…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — The University of Cebu (UC) Webmasters turned a highly anticipated marquee matchup into a one-sided affair, steamrolling the University of San Carlos (USC) Warriors, 81-63, in the Cebu Schools Athletic Foundation, Inc. (Cesafi) Season 26 men’s basketball tournament on Thursday night, Sept. 10, at the Cebu Coliseum.

The Webmasters improved to 2-0 to start the season, handing USC its first loss after the Warriors opened their campaign with an impressive victory over four-time defending champion University of the Visayas (UV) Green Lancers.

Ricofer Sordilla led the way for UC, catching fire from all areas of the floor to finish with a game-high 23 points. He shot 7-of-13 from the field, including 4-of-6 from beyond the arc, while adding three rebounds, two steals and an assist.
UC team captain Luther Leonard dominated the paint with a double-double of 17 points and 10 rebounds, along with four assists and a block.
Maverick Eligoyo also delivered another solid performance as UC’s third scoring option, contributing 16 points, five rebounds, two assists and a steal.
USC was led by James Paolo Gica, who scored 18 points on 7-of-17 shooting, including four 3-pointers. Jhoernel Tangkay added 15 points and seven rebounds, while RJ Enriquez finished with 10 points.
The Webmasters controlled the boards, 41-31, and eventually built their biggest lead of 18 points in the fourth quarter.
USC, however, gave UC a tough fight early, with the game featuring six lead changes and five deadlocks before the Webmasters began to pull away in the second period.
UC took a 40-31 lead into halftime and steadily extended its advantage in the second half to secure its second straight victory.

articles.title: Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with UAE
articles.summary: Algeria said that it was closing its airspace and severing ties with the United Arab Emirates. Algiers accuses Abu Dhabi of destabilizing countries such as Libya, Sudan and Mali.

image.caption: Algeria has severed ties with the UAE after years of tensions over Abu Dhabi's growing influence in AfricaImage: Fateh Guidoum/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Algeria severed diplomatic ties with the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, citing what it described as "provocative and hostile acts."
The Algerian Defense Ministry said the country would close its airspace to the UAE beginning on Friday.
However, commercial flights to and from Algiers will be allowed to continue until the end of 2026.
Relations between the two countries have been strained for years over the UAE's expanding influence in northern and western Africa.
What did Algeria and the UAE say about the decision?
The Algerian Foreign Ministry said that it had made the decision "after exhausting all avenues to preserve bilateral relations" with the Gulf country.
It added that the UAE had "persisted in its actions, reaching a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable."
Algiers said it had given the UAE's ambassador 48 hours to comply with the decision to cut ties.
The Emirati Foreign Ministry said that it hoped that the decision would be temporary.
"The UAE expresses hope that this decision will be temporary, in a manner that preserves the fraternal ties between the two brotherly peoples," the ministry said in a statement.

It said that it "affirms the UAE's appreciation for the brotherly Algerian people and its pride in the bonds ​that unite the two peoples, particularly through the Algerian community residing in the UAE and Algerian visitors."

Following the announcement, Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic advisor to UAE leader Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, said that diplomatic relations should be based on "rationality, communication and clarity of interests" rather than "riddles and signals that require decoding."
He did not explicitly mention Algeria in his post on X.

blocks.caption: Algerian President Abdelmajid Tebboune has accused the UAE of contributing to armed conflicts in the region [FILE: 18 August, 2024]Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What are the tensions between Algeria and the UAE?
Algeria has in the past accused Abu Dhabi of working to destabilize countries in northern Africa and the Sahel such as Libya, Mali, and Sudan.
The UAE has been accused of supporting the RSF paramilitary in Sudan's civil war, a charge it denies.
It also backs former warlord Khalifa Haftar's Tobruk-based administration in eastern Libya, a rival to the UN-recognized government in Tripoli.
In July, Algerian President Abdelmajid Tebboune harshly criticized the UAE for its influence in other countries, saying "wherever they set foot, blood flows."
"We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country."

Algeria also severed its diplomatic ties with neighboring Morocco in 2021, accusing Rabat of supporting Amazigh separatists in the coastal Kabylia region and amid longstanding tensions over the territory of Western Sahara.

articles.title: Trump ally resigns from post leading inquiry into alleged conspiracy against president
articles.summary:
Joe diGenova led investigation focused on intelligence assessment that Russia interfered in 2016 election

An ally of Donald…

blocks.text: An ally of Donald Trump said on Thursday that he has resigned from his post leading a Department of Justice investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president.
“I did in fact resign,” Joe diGenova told the Associated Press, calling it an “honor and a privilege” to serve Trump and the justice department.

He declined to comment on the circumstances of his departure, which came just five months after he was brought back to the justice department to help oversee a loosely defined investigation targeting former government officials who over the last decade have scrutinized Trump in various criminal inquiries.
A spokesperson for the justice department did not immediately return a message seeking comment.

The departure injects instant tumult into the investigation, which had shown recent signs of accelerating its pace with new subpoenas demanding testimony before a federal grand jury in Florida, where the investigation has been based.

The 81-year-old diGenova served as the US attorney for the District of Columbia during the Reagan administration. A close Trump ally, he was brought back to the justice department in April and given responsibility for an investigation aimed at trying to establish a conspiracy against Trump.
DiGenova had previously asked then US attorney general Pam Bondi to appoint him to the job and had openly and repeatedly claimed Trump was the victim of an intelligence community conspiracy.
Five months later, no charges have been brought and it remains unclear whether any will be, or what information – if any – has been gathered to support the idea of a conspiracy against Trump.
The investigation has focused intensely on one of Trump’s chief grievances: a US intelligence community assessment that Russia had interfered on his behalf in the 2016 presidential election.
after newsletter promotion

The president and some of his supporters have long decried that conclusion as a “deep state” plot to undermine the legitimacy of his win. Multiple government investigations, including by a justice department special counsel and by the department’s own inspector general, have concluded that Russia interfered in sweeping fashion to help get Trump elected.

The year-long investigation had proceeded in fits and starts well before diGenova’s appointment, which was announced soon after a career national security prosecutor who had been playing a key role in the investigation was replaced on the inquiry after raising doubts about its legal viability.

articles.title: Trump pledges $5,000 per adult if Republicans top midterms

blocks.text: President Donald Trump has pledged to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

The dubious promise would likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, and would further exacerbate the country’s nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and concerns about inflation.
Trump also said on Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after US midterm elections.

The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.
Joe Londsdale, a prominent Republican donor and activist, is among the Trump allies panning the president’s latest promise to send money directly to Americans.
“I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this (administration),” he wrote on X, “but am strongly against bread and circus bribes.”

It’s not just Republicans descending on Dallas for the midterm convention—Democrats are there too as they try to convince voters that the reality of Donald Trump’s second presidency doesn’t match the spectacle of his made-for-TV event. /das

articles.title: Anthropic says it blocked AI misuse linked to bioweapons
articles.summary: Anthropic said Thursday it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its artificial intelligence models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to…

blocks.text: Anthropic said Thursday it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its artificial intelligence models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to biological weapons.

As AI models grow more powerful, elaborate cyberattacks no longer require sophisticated skills and even lone individuals can create threats that would not have been possible even a year ago, Anthropic said. The company said it has added stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could also be used to make weapons.

“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic said in its third report since March 2025 describing AI misuse. The report includes snippets of the malicious code and AI prompts Anthropic said it found, and urges governments and AI competitors to identify and prevent similar abuse.

“We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services. As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” the company said.

The lengthy report by the AI startup, which is planning an initial public offering this fall, was published the day after one of its researchers announced he’s resigning over concerns that Anthropic and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development. He echoed concerns raised inside and outside of the industry about the technology’s potential to elude human control.
Claude was asked to support making a virus more harmful

Between December 2025 and August 2026, researchers at Anthropic found misuse by actors ranging from spyware vendors and “politically motivated individuals” to state-sponsored groups spreading propaganda.

Among the findings in the company’s report are unnamed actors attempting to use its models for research that could have led to biological weapons. In one instance, Anthropic said its systems blocked a request for Claude’s assistance in authoring a grant application for scientific funding.

“The work discussed in the application involved gain-of-function research (that is, research that genetically alters an organism to create a new or enhanced biological property) on the chikungunya virus. This gain of function research was aimed at the virus’ transmissibility and immune evasion properties,” the report said.

Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes debilitating symptoms such as severe pain and fever. The request involved a grant proposal for research seeking to enhance mutations to make the virus progressively more harmful. While such research could “certainly” be used to develop better vaccines and treatments, Anthropic said, “it could also be used to make the pathogen more dangerous.”
Anthropic says it can’t claim its models do no harm

None of the cases Anthropic included in its report were found to be using its newer, more powerful Claude Fable or Mythos-class models, with the exception of one illicit distillation case that Anthropic described as “an industrial-scale, covert campaign to extract a model’s capabilities and replicate them in another model without authorization.”

Anthropic said its older models, such as Claude Opus 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, from 2025, “were well below the threshold where they could meaningfully assist a sophisticated user in carrying out dangerous biological research.”

“As a result, safeguards on these models were less stringent, directed mostly at preventing access to content that might uplift novices in recreating known bioweapons,” the report said. “But for today’s models—which are capable of assisting in a range of complex scientific research tasks — the evidence is no longer certain, and we cannot make that same assurance.”

Because of this, Anthropic has applied “stronger safeguards that restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries” in its more recent models, such as Claude Fable 5, the report said.
Report follows a researcher’s dire warning

Anthropic also found groups that created hundreds of social media accounts that look like they belong to ordinary people and then posted material amplifying the same political view over the course of a week. The company outlined nine such cases it found, originating in Russia, Iran, Turkey and across the Persian Gulf, South Asia, Africa and Europe.
While social media companies can detect influence operations on their platforms once posts are circulating, “we may see it on Claude while the operation is still being built.”

Anthropic released this report after one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, announced he’s resigning amid fears the company and its chief rival OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s post warned that some of his colleagues now believe AI could threaten human life by the end of the decade.

But Anthropic said it has blocked each of the malicious activities it identified, used the experience to strengthen safeguards and shared information with government authorities and industry partners.

“We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses,” Anthropic said. /das

articles.title: Senate panel approves PH SOVFA with France
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said on Thursday the Philippines has “no choice” but to expand its defense partnerships as its territory comes under pressure from China,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said on Thursday the Philippines has “no choice” but to expand its defense partnerships as its territory comes under pressure from China, as a Senate committee approved a proposed visiting forces agreement with France.
According to Teodoro, having more defense partners would strengthen the country’s deterrence.

“For the Philippines, we view it as a matter of no choice because our territories are under severe stress, to put it politely, by the unilateral and illegal acts of China,” he told senators during a hearing.
“Thus, we cannot deny the fact that as many coalition partners we have, it adds to our deterrent posture in this country,” Teodoro said.
Legal framework

The Senate committee on foreign relations chaired by Sen. Juan Miguel Zubiri approved the Philippines-France Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (Sovfa). clearing the way for its endorsement to the plenary.

The pact, the country’s first with a European nation, establishes a legal framework for the presence and activities of visiting Filipino and French defense personnel in each other’s territory, subject to its provisions and the countries’ domestic approval processes.
Teodoro said France was an important strategic partner because it is both a European and Pacific power, with territories in the Pacific, including New Caledonia and French Polynesia.

He also pointed to France’s support for the Philippines’ 2016 arbitral award on the South China Sea and its commitment to freedom of navigation and international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
At the same time, Teodoro said he expected China to maintain its increasingly assertive behavior in the West Philippine Sea and urged the Philippines and its partners to change how they respond.

“I think we will see more of the same. We should not expect any change in their behavior; what we should change is the way we react,” Teodoro said at the 2nd Manila Strategy Forum in Parañaque City, also on Thursday.

He cited China’s activities in the West Philippine Sea, including what he described as harassment of Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and naval vessels and aircraft, as well as its recent announcement of plans to establish a marine observatory at Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal).
Chinese forces, meanwhile, twice fired flares on Monday at an unarmed PCG plane on a routine surveillance flight over the Kalayaan Island Group before landing on Pag-asa Island.

The PCG reported the incident on Thursday, saying that People’s Liberation Army forces at Zamora (Subi) Reef first challenged its aircraft over the radio before firing flares in its direction—a tactic they repeated shortly after at Panganiban (Mischief) Reef.

The Coast Guard said the incident raised flight safety concerns, adding that the discharge of flares against an aircraft in flight disregarded the duty of due regard under the Convention on International Civil Aviation. — With a report from Keith Clores /das

articles.title: More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’
articles.summary:
Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’

A day after a former researcher at Anthropic made an apocalyptic declaration…

blocks.text: A day after a former researcher at Anthropic made an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings.
In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”.

The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but haven’t said so publicly.

These researchers and staff are posting in response to a now-viral thread from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who said on Wednesday he was resigning from the company because neither Anthropic nor its competitor OpenAI, also his former employer, were building AI models responsibly and are “gambling with our lives”.

Anna Wang, who works on Artificial General Intelligence Safety at Anthropic and previously worked at Google’s DeepMind, said Thursday that many people at Anthropic want to slow down development to come up with a plan to mitigate the risks that could come with these AI models.
“There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI,” Wang wrote on X.
Drake Thomas, another Anthropic employee, said that he respected Coxon’s choice to abstain from building these models if he worries they could pose planet-scale risks.
“Things are moving way too fast, we don’t have anywhere near the degree of assurance we’ll want for ASI [artificial superintelligence],” Thomas said.
Musk took a more adversarial stance. “Seems like a setup,” he wrote.
Coxon replied to the world’s richest man with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my real beliefs. You could ask your xAI researchers about me if you hadn’t fired them.”

In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said.

Musk and others with a more positive view of AI have started to spread theories that Coxon’s post and the resulting fallout are part of a “psyop” to negatively influence the public’s feelings about AI.
“I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk posted on X. “This was just the match that lit the fire.”

Musk was responding to a post by Parker Thayer, a researcher at conservativethinktank Capital Research, in which he floated a theory with little evidence that Coxon’s post was the start of a “VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion”. Other notable figures took notice.
after newsletter promotion
Bill Ackman, the billionaire CEO of the hedge fund Pershing Square, also quoted Thayer’s post, simply saying “Interesting.”
Other Anthropic employees had posted their agreement with Coxon shortly after he declared his resignation on Wednesday.

“AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Samuel Marks, who works on safety research at Anthropic. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.”

Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said Coxon was “correct” and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.

It’s not exactly clear how Coxon and others expect AI models to usher in the demise of humanity. Some experts doubt that the technology will become so intelligent as to cause the apocalypse. Gary Marcus, a scientist and leading voice in AI, said that it’s time to boycott AI, but because it’s already causing harm.

More than extinction, Marcus said he worried about the “risk of catastrophe” from “from AI-generated pathogens, from wars started or escalated by AI-generated disinformation, from hacks that destroy critical infrastructure, and so on. Nothing I have seen gives any indication that any of that is under control”.
The same day, Anthropic released a report documenting how the company dismantled an operation attempting to build a biological weapon using its AI models.

articles.title: Family of teen struck at Toronto intersection where speed camera was removed sues province, city and driver
articles.summary: The family of a teen struck by a driver at a Toronto intersection that used to have an automated speed enforcement (ASE) camera before Ontario passed legislation to remove it is suing the province,…

image.caption: A City of Toronto speed camera on Parkside Avenue. Earlier this year, a 15-year-old teen was struck by a driver and suffered serious injuries at a different intersection after a speed camera there was removed. His family is now suing the city, province and the driver. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

The family of a teen struck by a driver at a Toronto intersection that used to have an automated speed enforcement (ASE) camera before Ontario passed legislation to remove it is suing the province, city and driver for millions of dollars in damages.
Teen suffered 'permanent, serious disfigurement,' lawsuit alleges

On March 25, Toronto police said they responded to calls for a pedestrian struck at the intersection of Humber Boulevard N. and Louvain Street. A 15-year-old boy was rushed to hospital with life-threatening injuries, according to police.
The driver, a 71-year-old man, remained at the scene.
He was arrested and charged with dangerous operation and careless driving causing bodily harm, police said in an email Thursday.

items: Toronto saw significant increase in speeders after camera removals: city report

blocks.text: A statement of claim, dated Sept. 3, filed at the Ontario Superior Court by the teen's family and parents, Adebola and Taiwo Adebayo, alleges their son sustained "serious disfigurement and permanent serious impairment of an important physical, mental and psychological function."

The teen suffered a traumatic brain injury, several skull fractures, injury to a carotid artery, loss of vision in the right eye, fractures to his left femur (thigh bone) and "various lacerations, abrasions and contusions" to his body, according to the statement of claim.
The injuries have caused ongoing psychological and behavioural changes, including anxiety, depression and emotional trauma, according to the claim.

The Adebayos' son will "continue to sustain pain and suffering, a loss of enjoyment of life and a loss of amenities," it said, noting that he will need to undergo therapy, rehabilitation and use specialized equipment.
No comment from province, lawsuit alleges it allowed 'dangerous situation'

The statement of claim alleges that neither the city or the province equipped the intersection of Humber Boulevard N. and Louvain Street with "protective measures," such as a traffic signal or raised crosswalk, after the speed camera in that area was taken down.

The speed camera at the intersection operated from around April 2025 until November 2025, according to the claim. The Ford government's Bill 56, which gained royal assent in November 2025, mandated the removal of speed cameras across the province, which Ford had called a "cash grab."

items: All of Toronto's speed cameras are gone. How did we get to this point?

blocks.text: As a result, the province "created and allowed a situation of danger to exist" at the intersection, the lawsuit alleges.
It also says the province ignored complaints about the intersection and "took no or inadequate steps to remedy the situation."
Ontario's Ministry of Transportation declined to provide comment, saying the matter is before the court.
Ford to ban speed cameras in Ontario
The intersection where the teen was struck serves as a pedestrian path to a high school in the area, St. Oscar Romero Catholic Secondary School.
Patrick Brown, one of the lawyers representing the teen and his family, told CBC News part of the claim is based on "operational negligence."
"We are alleging that after removing cameras, they [the province] failed to replace it with other protective measures in a known hazardous area," he said in an email Thursday.
City says 'hearts are with the teen and his family'

The statement of claim alleges multiple requests were sent by an "area resident" to Toronto's 311 service, asking the city to assess the safety of pedestrian paths students use to get to the school, including the one where the teen was struck.

The city "knew, or ought to have known" the crossing was hazardous to pedestrians, but it failed to "take reasonable steps to ensure the safety of pedestrians crossing the intersection," the statement of claim said.
In an emailed statement Thursday, city spokesperson Russell Baker said "our hearts are with the teen and his family."

"While speed cameras helped reduce speeding, the City of Toronto continues to prioritize the safety of all road users through other measures in the Vision Zero program. Some of these tools include Community and School Safety Zones, safety signage, pavement markings, pedestrian head start signals, and red-light cameras," he said.
The family is seeking $16 million in damages.

items: Toronto sees 28% jump in traffic fatalities in 2026 compared to last year: police data

blocks.text: ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alina Snisarenko is a Toronto-based journalist. She currently works as a digital writer for CBC Toronto and has previously worked as an associate producer with CBC Radio's Metro Morning. You can reach her with story ideas or tips at alina.snisarenko@cbc.ca.
With files from Jasmin Seputis

articles.title: San Francisco mayor declares rent emergency as housing costs soar
articles.summary:
Median rent for one-bedroom apartment in city tops $4,495 with a national median of $1,900

San Francisco’s mayor, Daniel…

blocks.text: San Francisco’s mayor, Daniel Lurie, declared a rent emergency on Thursday, proposing reforms aimed at curbing evictions and preventing rent spikes as the city grapples with soaring apartment prices.
The Bay Area city, home to a large number of high-earning tech workers, has long been one of the most expensive housing and rental markets in the country.

The median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in San Francisco is currently $4,495, according to Zumper, a rental listings site. In comparison, the national median for a one-bedroom apartment is $1,900.

The ballooning rental costs have been attributed to a recent influx of wealth in the market, as artificial intelligence companies began to go public on the stock market. While demand has ratcheted up for limited housing options, San Francisco has notoriously lagged behind other cities in approving new housing.

Among Lurie’s proposed measures are caps to rent increases for rent-controlled apartments, $27m in funding to cover funding lapses from federal housing vouchers set to expire and an increase in payments to tenants who are evicted under the Ellis Act, legislation landlords can evoke when leaving the rental business.
“Today, most San Franciscans feel our city is finally moving in the right direction, but many are also asking whether they can still afford to live here,” Lurie said in a statement on Thursday.

“We have lived through booms before – this time, we have an opportunity to build a recovery that is broad-based and lasting, where San Franciscans can put down roots and participate in our city’s success.”

articles.title: First phase of Army restructuring creates division focused on defending Canada
articles.summary: Canada's Army formally made one of the biggest changes to its structure in decades Thursday by shifting from divisions based on geography to ones built around specific purposes. A new division, that…

image.caption: The Canadian Army has created a new division, headquartered in Edmonton, that will help it to deploy rapidly. It's part of a series of structural changes ordered by Lt.-Gen. Michael Wright, who laid out his plan to modernize the army in 2025. (Cpl Myki Poirier-Joyal/Department of National Defence)

blocks.text: Edmonton

Canada's Army formally made one of the biggest changes to its structure in decades Thursday by shifting from divisions based on geography to ones built around specific purposes. A new division, that prepares the army to rapidly deploy, will be headquartered in Edmonton.
New division that prepares the army to rapidly deploy will be headquartered in Edmonton
Canada's Army formally made one of the biggest changes to its structure in decades Thursday by shifting from divisions based on geography to ones built around specific purposes.

Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Edmonton held a signing ceremony and parade to stand up the 1st Canadian Division, which will serve as the main force responsible for deploying on large-scale combat operations and responding to crises.
Headquartered in Edmonton, the "manoeuvre division" will bring multiple capabilities together under one roof, including tanks and other armour, artillery, light infantry, paratroopers and engineers.
The idea is to prepare the army to rapidly deploy a large force and sustain prolonged operations.
"This is a big change," Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the new 1st Canadian Division, said in an interview.
"This is not an exercise in restructuring the deck chairs. We're doing this in order to be more agile, more lethal, more relevant to defend Canada."
Rutland said the threat environment has changed and the world is returning to large-scale combat operations with hundreds of thousands of soldiers, like the ones in Ukraine.

"We realized that we needed to stand up what we call a war fighting division, which will bring together thousands of troops able to integrate air, cyber, space effects and actually contribute as a really trusted ally into that likely future fight," he said.
It's part of a series of structural changes ordered by Lt.-Gen. Michael Wright, who laid out his plan to modernize the army in a 2025 document titled Inflection Point.

items: Canadian Army overhaul looms as DND finalizes mobilization plans

blocks.text: Alongside the manoeuvre division, the army is setting up a support division, which will be run out of Kingston, Ont.

The army also is standing up a "defence of Canada" division based out of Montreal, to be known as the 2nd Canadian Division. It's made up largely of part-time soldiers and will focus on national emergencies and domestic defence.
The 3rd Canadian Division — which traces its history to the First World War and took part in the 1944 D-Day landing at Juno Beach — is being retired to the supplementary Order of Battle.
This retirement happens when a regiment is powered down but continues to exist administratively in case it needs to be returned to duty.
The 3rd's regular force troops will go into the 1st Division, its reserves and rangers will go into the 2nd division and its support troops will join the support division.

Under the changes, the 1st Canadian Division — a division that dates back to 1915 and helped to capture Vimy Ridge — will command three Canadian Mechanized Brigade Groups, located in Edmonton, Petawawa, Ont., and at CFB Valcartier in Quebec.
It also will oversee the 3rd Light Infantry Regiment, the Canadian Artillery Brigade, 6 Canadian Combat Support Brigade and 1 Canadian Sustainment Brigade.

"It means a lot to us," Rutland said. "You know, the 1st Division was the first one into the fight in the Second World War. They were the first ones in major combat in Italy, Sicily, in the Second World War."

articles.title: Man accused in Mexican condo scheme claims he was a victim, too
articles.summary: A U.K. man facing accusations he took part in a scheme that wiped out a Canadian couple's retirement savings says he's provided proof to Mexican authorities probing the case that he never touched a…

image.caption: Harry Robinson says he's provided proof to Mexican authorities that he never touched the funds he and his co-accused are alleged to have defrauded from an Ontario couple as part of a condo-flipping scheme in Mexico. (Jorge Barrera/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New

A U.K. man facing accusations he took part in a scheme that wiped out a Canadian couple's retirement savings says he's provided proof to Mexican authorities probing the case that he never touched a dime of the vanished funds, and that he's also a victim of his co-accused.
Harry Robinson says he never touched Canadian couple's lost retirement savings
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 10, 2026 5:22 PM EDT | Last Updated: 28 minutes ago

Harry Robinson, 66, is accused of working with a Mexican national named Jacqueline Herrera Herrera to defraud Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown of Curve Lake, Ont., of $280,000 by offering them a fake deal to buy and flip seven condos.

Robinson provided CBC News with a memo and HSBC bank records, both filed with the state attorney general's office of Quintana Roo, that he says proves Herrera redirected Thompson and Brown's money — sent over three installments — through cashier's cheques and transfers to other, unknown accounts.

The memo, filed Aug. 24, alleges that Herrera had total control over the account which was under the name of Xen Investments, their former joint venture. It claims Herrera put the account under a "lock" to prevent Robinson from accessing or moving funds.
CBC News was not provided with any documented proof outlining the alleged lock on the account.
The memo asks state investigators to seek a judicial order to obtain the names linked to the cashier's cheques and other bank accounts to trace the final destination of the funds.

"If you watch any criminal show on TV, the one statement that is made all the time: Follow the money," Robinson told CBC News in his real-estate office in Puerto Morelos, a small port town between the tourist hotspots Playa del Carmen and Cancun.
"And yet, here we are in a fraud case with missing money and no one has made any attempt to follow the money."

However, state authorities are not focusing their case against Robinson and Herrera on what happened to the money, according to other court records. There have been no applications yet before the courts to trace the movement of Thompson and Brown's funds after they landed in Xen Investments's account.

The investigation is simply focused on proving there was fraud by deceit — that Herrera and Robinson did not have any access or control over the seven condos they offered Thompson and Brown as part of a deal, which promised the couple 100 per cent profit.

"This operation evolved as more resources were collected, without the existence … availability or actual allocation of the promised units being documentally proven," says a state prosecutor's filing seeking arrest warrants against Herrera and Robinson, which was obtained by CBC News.
"For months [Thompson and Brown] were kept in a narrative of extensions, new fund requests … and imminent refunds that never materialized."

A state judge issued those warrants on July 24. Herrera and Robinson both obtained stays in Mexican federal court against the warrants, but their state-level criminal proceedings are waiting on a judge to set a date to commence.
"I don't think I'm being fairly treated … by the prosecutor's office. I think they're not going after the true criminal in this case," said Robinson.
"I've lived my whole life honest, no problems, no criminal record, nothing … and all of a sudden I'm now some sort of master criminal? Nobody makes that transition like that."

Publicly available records show Robinson was born in Liverpool and that he worked in Australia and the U.S. before moving to Mexico. CBC News could find no evidence of any sanctions against Robinson or court cases involving him or his businesses.
Robinson says he moved to Mexico around 2020 and also has Australian citizenship.
A fraud by deceit conviction could lead to a prison sentence ranging between three to 12 years.
Robinson says he's asked the U.K. Embassy for help.
The 'middleman'
Thompson said that Robinson was the "middleman" throughout the months of attempted dealmaking, which started in 2024.
"I had 100 per cent faith in [Robinson]," she said.

"He was very convincing … anytime we had any questions or concerns, he always had an answer … I would get: ‘relax, calm down, everything's going to be fine, it's just taking a long time. It's Mexico, right?'"
Robinson says he was also duped by Herrera and believed the deal was real — though he put none of his own money into the pot, despite telling Thompson he would also go in as an investor.
"The deal was that all my time and effort, everything else, was going to be paid in commission. That commission was set aside and put toward the deal," he said.
"And I would see it one day. So I didn't even get anything upfront."

Robinson said he met Herrera around three or four years ago and attended several private events with her and that she seemed to be well connected and respected as a Cancun realtor with 30 years of experience.

"Everybody seemed to now have gone out of their way to tell me how good a person Jacqueline was, how trustworthy she was, how I couldn't have found a better business partner," said Robinson. "I was a mark in exactly the same way [Thompson] was."
Seeking settlement

Herrera claims Robinson also took some of Thompson and Brown's money. She is seeking to avoid criminal proceedings by offering to repay part of the missing money through an alternative justice channel that is part of the Mexican system.

Herrera is offering to repay $2.4 million pesos — roughly $196,000 — in two installments to Thompson and Brown under a court-authorized settlement. Herrera has claimed — through her lawyer, according to Thompson — that Robinson is responsible for the rest.

items: Arrest warrants issued in Mexico for duo accused in alleged condo scam
Mexican authorities probe alleged scam that wiped out Canadian couple’s retirement savings

blocks.text: Herrera declined an interview request, but told CBC News it was "never" her intention to defraud Thompson and Brown.
Thompson and Brown say they are facing a tough decision on whether to proceed with Herrera's settlement offer.
"Our biggest worry is, if we accept that, do we get the rest of the money?" said Brown.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jorge Barrera is a Caracas-born journalist currently based in Mexico City for CBC News. He previously worked with CBC's Investigative Unit and CBC's Indigenous Unit. Follow him on X @JorgeBarrera or email him jorge.barrera@cbc.ca.

articles.title: From pipelines, to railways and AI: Ottawa pitches 167 projects ahead of Carney's investment summit
articles.summary: CBC News has obtained the federal government's "prospectus" detailing investment opportunities ahead of next week's Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, which includes various plans across eight…

image.caption: Mark Carney takes part in a press conference at the Davie shipyard in Lévis, QC. August 24, 2026. Ahead of the Prime Minister's investment summit, CBC News obtained a copy of the prospectus document outlining the projects that will be pitched to investors. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Business·New

CBC News has obtained the federal government's "prospectus" detailing investment opportunities ahead of next week's Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, which includes various plans across eight areas of investment.
Next week's summit aims to attract $1 trillion in international investment to Canada
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 10, 2026 5:20 PM EDT | Last Updated: 10 minutes ago

A floating LNG terminal on B.C.'s coast, a high-speed rail line between Edmonton and Calgary and a pipeline from Alberta to the Pacific Ocean are among 167 possible investment opportunities Prime Minister Mark Carney will show off at next week's investment summit in Toronto.

The projects are outlined in a 66-page "prospectus" obtained by CBC News, which gives the most detailed look yet at the investment opportunities Ottawa and Canadian business leaders plan to showcase at the summit.

The Sept. 14 and 15 gathering, hosted by the prime minister in partnership with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Public Sector Pension Investment Board, will bring together deep-pocketed international investors and Canadian business leaders in hopes of drumming up $1 trillion in investment.

CBC News previously reported that invitations went out to some of the world's biggest investment firms and sovereign wealth funds as part of a broader push to attract capital at a time of trade upheaval and geopolitical uncertainty.
With the U.S.-Canada trade war escalating, the government is also under pressure to deepen economic ties beyond the United States.

items: Carney's pitch to unlock trillions in global investment

blocks.text: The document groups the pitches into eight areas of investment: 11 conventional energy projects, 31 clean energy projects, 63 in mining and metals, 16 in marine and port infrastructure, 11 in power and utilities, 10 in digital technology, 19 in advanced manufacturing and six transportation projects.
Each pitch highlights the project's current stage, the capital expenditure needed and the kind of investment being sought to help it get built.

Some of the priciest projects on the list include a $57 billion US expansion of the Port of Churchill; a $44 billion investment in Nova Scotia's Wind West offshore wind project, led by the province; the proposed $35 billion West Coast Oil Pipeline, which would carry oil from Alberta to B.C.'s coast; and the $28.5 billion Ksi Lisims LNG terminal project.
Canada reaches large-scale deal to export LNG to Germany: sources

Other projects include a float glass manufacturing facility in Manitoba, expanded manufacturing capacity for night-vision technology used in defence and satellite technology for Earth observation, along with the long list of infrastructure projects.

Absent from the list are the Alto high-speed rail project, which would run between Toronto and Quebec City and has received pushback over the land expropriation it would require, and any plans to privatize airports, which Carney's government has been weighing.

Some projects are also closer to reality than others. The Ksi Lisims project, for example, is described as "fully permitted and shovel ready," while a critical-mineral graphite project in Saskatchewan is listed as being in the preliminary stages of economic and environmental assessment.

The prospectus spells out plans for a $57 billion US expansion to the Port of Churchill. Upgrades to Canada's only deepwater Arctic seaport would include a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export corridor, rail upgrades and other modernization aimed at establishing a "four-season trade gateway."

items: Carney names Dominic Barton as chair of Invest in Canada, replaces CEO

blocks.text: For Alberta, the prospectus spells out a $10.9 billion plan for a high-speed passenger rail line linking Calgary and Edmonton. The document says trains would reach speeds of more than 300 kilometres per hour, completing the trip in about 90 minutes.
For the oil and gas sector, plans include a $35 billion, 1,250-kilometre-long oil pipeline connecting Alberta crude production to a deepwater export terminal in southern British Columbia.

The document also includes a $2.1 billion US proposal for Calgary-based South Bow's Prairie Connector pipeline expansion. The proposal would add 380 kilometres of new pipeline to transport Canadian crude to U.S. refining markets in the Midwest. Prairie Connector would use parts of the cancelled Keystone XL pipeline previously built on the Canadian side of the border.

For natural gas, the document includes a $28.5 billion pitch for the floating Ksi Lisims LNG export facility on the B.C. coast. Currently, 99 per cent of Canada's natural gas exports are destined for the United States. Amid ongoing trade tension, Carney's government has sought to diversify the pool of buyers for Canada's energy exports.

In clean energy, the federal government is attempting to sell investors on access to "the world's cleanest and most reliable energy systems." Proposals span nuclear power generation in New Brunswick, carbon capture in Saskatchewan, and wind power and green hydrogen in Newfoundland and Labrador.
Aside from natural resources and hard infrastructure, the document frames Canada as a pioneer in artificial intelligence, with a national strategy dating back to 2017.

Investment opportunities in this sector include a $14.5 billion data centre near Medicine Hat, Alta., along with several smaller data centre projects. The prospectus also offers investors an opportunity to invest in Toronto-based Xanadu Quantum Technologies, which makes quantum computers powered by light instead of electricity.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.
With files from Kate McKenna

articles.title: AP journalists who witnessed 9/11 remember what they saw, 25 years later
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Karen Matthews was getting her 3-year-old daughter ready for preschool in her Manhattan apartment on Sept. 11, 2001, when she heard a loud boom, unlike anything she’d ever heard before.…

blocks.text: NEW YORK — Karen Matthews was getting her 3-year-old daughter ready for preschool in her Manhattan apartment on Sept. 11, 2001, when she heard a loud boom, unlike anything she’d ever heard before.
Holding her child, she went outside. Around her, people stared up at a gash in the north tower of the World Trade Center, smoke billowing from the building just blocks from her home.

“What did you see? What did you see?” people were asking one another. Matthews, an Associated Press reporter, began asking the same question, fumbling to get out her notebook and record what people had witnessed, all with her daughter still in her arms.

Matthews had planned to drop her daughter at school before working later to cover New York’s primary election. Instead, she and other AP journalists found themselves documenting the Sept. 11 attacks as they lived through them.
Twenty-five years later, they remember what they saw.
At first, no one knew what was happening
On her way outside, Matthews passed a woman in her building’s lobby with tears streaming down her face. Some people assumed a small plane had accidentally struck the tower.
Then she saw a “big fireball” erupt from the south tower as a second hijacked jet struck.
“‘I want to go to school, I want to go to school,’” her daughter started crying.
“That’s when we all knew that we were under attack,” Matthews said.

Matthews started toward the preschool anyway, until she saw teachers grabbing children and running north, many of them crying. She took her daughter upstairs, intent on getting her to a safe place, and put on Barney.

Then she heard two more impossibly loud roars — one tower collapsing, then the other. Nearly 3,000 people died in the World Trade Center, at the Pentagon, and on the four jets hijacked by al-Qaida militants.
Twenty-five years later, Matthews, now retired, still divides her life into before Sept. 11 and after.
“I’m not a really fearful person,” she said. “But you lose a sense of security when something like that happens.”
“I do think it helped to be part of telling the story of what happened,” Matthews said.
The camera becomes a wall
Lower Manhattan’s streets were filled with smoke and debris when Richard Drew got off the subway at Chambers Street and saw the burning twin towers.
His assignment that day had originally been to cover the opening day of Fashion Week — a whirlwind of glamour, models and runway shows.
He began taking pictures. Gray ash and soot covered his clothes, face and cameras.
An emergency medical worker pointed up and said, “Look at that.” People were plummeting from the burning towers.
“I don’t know whether they were jumping or they got forced out by the fire,” Drew said.

Drew photographed them. One image became known as “The Falling Man.” It shows a lone man falling headfirst, his body nearly aligned with the vertical lines of the towers. The photograph appeared in some newspapers the next day, but was rejected by other publications that worried readers would find it too upsetting.
Drew still thinks about the photograph — and the unidentified man in it — at least once a week.

“When I’m in a situation like September 11th, I go into professional photographer mode and I concentrate on whatever’s happening in front of me,” said Drew, who also photographed the 1968 assassination of Robert F. Kennedy.
He said his wife calls his camera a wall — a filter between the photographer and the reality they’re capturing.
“I guess I’m in denial about whether those things really affected me,” he said.
The wheelchairs stayed empty
Dust from the pulverized towers was falling “like a snowstorm” when AP reporter Larry Neumeister made it to a hospital near ground zero that afternoon.
Doctors and nurses gathered outside. Lines of wheelchairs and gurneys waited at the entrance. Staff were preparing for a constant stream of injured survivors — potentially thousands, Neumeister said.
Then the hours passed.
“It became clear nobody else was being brought in,” Neumeister said.

Around midnight, Neumeister walked by the World Trade Center site. A doctor told him: “You either walked away from the site or ran away from the World Trade Center buildings when they fell, or you were gone. There was no in-between.”
He knew his father’s voice
AP journalist Jeremy Brown, then 26, was filming near the World Trade Center when he heard a deep rumble. A firefighter ran toward him, yelling: “Grab your camera, follow me.”
Brown followed him into the loading dock of 7 World Trade Center as a huge wave of debris approached. They sheltered in a room as the building went dark.
“You could feel the heat from the debris. You could smell it,” Brown said.
When the rumbling stopped, they felt their way through the darkness until they found an emergency exit. Brown pulled his T-shirt over his face and began filming.
“Jeremy!” he suddenly heard someone shout. It was his father, who worked nearby.
“It was just incredible. It was like winning the lottery,” Brown said.
With no cell service, Brown’s mother didn’t know whether either had survived. Father and son stayed together that day, his father carrying Brown’s camera bag with extra tapes and batteries.

“As a cameraman that day, I was looking through my viewfinder, and everything was black and white, and I knew I was recording history,” Brown said. “But every time I looked up as a human I could see the devastation, the hurt, and I knew that the world was never going to be the same.”
Her training took over
Sept. 11 was supposed to be Amy Sancetta’s day off.
The Ohio-based retired AP photographer had stayed in New York after covering the U.S. Open tennis when her editor called: A small plane had hit one of the towers. She needed to go downtown.
Sancetta realized she didn’t know where the twin towers were. She got into a cab and told the driver to get her as close as he could.
About a block and a half away, Sancetta was photographing the south tower when it began to collapse.
“The weirdest thing that went through my head at the time was, it was kind of muscle memory, like shooting a basketball game,” she said.

When the cloud of debris came toward her, Sancetta ran into a parking garage. In a stairwell, she found a woman crying who had escaped from the towers and wanted to call her son. Sancetta hugged her and reached for her flip phone. Her hand was shaking. There was no signal. Sancetta took the son’s number and promised to call him.

When she emerged onto the street, everything was white, “like covered with snow, but not snow.” The screaming and pounding footsteps had given way to crying and whimpering. Loose-leaf office paper floated through the sky “like birds.”
“I wish I’d shot that,” Sancetta said. “I didn’t, but I can see it — I see it right now.”
Twenty-five years later, Sancetta held up a newspaper from Sept. 12 showing the burning towers she had photographed.
“NIGHTMARE,” the headline read.
Outside her windows now are woods. But she can still remember the sound of the tower collapsing — “just unearthly.”
“As a journalist, I’m glad I was there,” Sancetta said. “But as a human being, I wish I’d gone home on Monday.” /das

articles.title: New battery-powered trains will ‘bring faster journeys to north’
articles.summary:
No 10 says 29 new trains to be built in Derby will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK

No 10 has announced the construction of a new fleet of battery-powered trains…

blocks.text: No 10 has announced the construction of a new fleet of battery-powered trains that will “bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north”.

The 29 new trains, which will be run by TransPennine Express, are set to be built in Alstom’s Litchurch Lane works in Derby from 2028, which the government says will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK.

The new fleet will be made up of Adessia Stream trains, a battery-powered model that will be the first of its kind to be used for long-distance mainline journeys in the UK when it enters service in 2034.

Prime minister Andy Burnham, who uses trains regularly to move between London and Manchester, highlighted the need for more reliable and efficient services, with the new trains pitched as making journeys between major northern cities shorter while increasing capacity on rail networks by 30% in the next decade.

Burnham said: “I’ve lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came. And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments and missed opportunities.
“Today that starts to change. These 29 new trains will bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north, and thousands of British jobs for the next generation.
“It’s exactly what Great British Railways is all about – taking back control of the basics and getting Britain believing again.”
As well as speed and capacity, the new trains are set to run without emissions even on non-electrified stretches of the network, while also having more accessible step-free boarding and onboard wifi.

Transport secretary Heidi Alexander also praised the announcement, calling it a sign of how Great British Railways “will deliver better journeys for people while backing British business” and allowing passengers to “wave goodbye to overcrowded, delayed diesel trains and step onboard faster electric trains which are fit for the future”.

articles.title: Coach crash kills several people in Swiss Alps
articles.summary: A coach carrying 48 Dutch passengers overturns, leaving several people dead.

blocks.text: A tourist coach has crashed in the south-eastern Swiss Alps, leaving several people dead and several injured, local police say.
The bus overturned between Susch and Zernez in the Graubünden - also known as Grisons - region late on Thursday afternoon.
A large team of rescuers equipped with several helicopters was deployed to the scene.
Some 48 Dutch passengers were on board the bus, according to a spokeswoman for the General Dutch Association of Travel Companies on behalf of tour operator OAD.
The spokesperson told Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf they could not yet say how many people had been killed or injured.
Images on Swiss news sites show a coach lying on its side beside a narrow country road on which stand numerous ambulances while groups of rescuers work at the scene.
The coach reportedly left the Netherlands on Monday and was on a day trip to Switzerland from Austria when the crash happened.
Zernez is the entry point for visitors to the Swiss National Park, a vast Alpine reserve stretching more than 100 sq km (40 sq miles) across the mountainous Engadine valley.

articles.title: Australia news live: Anthony Albanese marks 25 years since September 11; aged care provider pays back thousands to residents
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

Good morning

Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live news coverage for Friday.

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese marks September 11 anniversary
Anthony Albanese has marked 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks in the US.
Ten Australians were among 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks in New York, Washington DC and in Pennsylvania – “lives tragically cut short far from home”.

double quotation markWe acknowledge the grief carried by their loved ones. We also honour the courage and selflessness shown in the face of unimaginable horror. First responders ran towards danger to help others. Ordinary people reached for one another. In the worst of circumstances, we saw extraordinary acts of courage, compassion and humanity.
The prime minister said the anniversary was also an opportunity to reflect on “resilience in the face of profound loss”.
double quotation markAustralia remembers those whose lives were taken, those who survived, those we’ve lost since, and all those who continue to carry the weight of that day.
Key events

items: 20m agoAnthony Albanese marks September 11 anniversary

blocks.text: Good morning
Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live news coverage for Friday.
Let’s begin.
Opal Healthcare refunds residents after review into misuse of aged care standards
Opal Healthcare has refunded roughly $190,000 to almost 350 residents under a sweeping review into misuse of new aged care standards, AAP reports.
The standards came into effect in November and were designed to give residents more say over what premium products they opted to pay for.
Guidelines said services that were previously offered for free could not be charged, though they were not made law.
Reports emerged months later of aged care providers wrongfully charging residents for basic amenities, including television and wifi services.
In some cases, services were removed if they were not paid for.
An investigation was launched by the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission after the aged care minister, Sam Rae, informed the regulator of claims against Opal Healthcare.
He said at the time the removal of services such as air conditioning and televisions was unacceptable.

articles.title: Harry Styles expands tour, will play Rogers Stadium in Toronto for two dates in 2027
articles.summary: Harry Styles has announced an expansion of his Together, Together 2027 tour, which will see him come to Toronto for two dates at Rogers Stadium.

image.caption: Harry Styles performs during the Brit Awards 2026 in Manchester, England, on Feb. 28. (Scott A. Garfitt/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Harry Styles has announced an expansion of his Together, Together 2027 tour, which will see him come to Toronto for two dates at Rogers Stadium.
The British singer has announced dates in 12 more cities for his Together, Together 2027 tour
Harry Styles will be bringing his tour to Canada next year — but only for two dates in Toronto.

The British pop star announced an expansion of his Together, Together tour into 2027 on Thursday, revealing that he will be coming to 12 more cities, starting with Phoenix on April 2, and ending with three dates in London at the end of August.
He will be performing at Rogers Stadium on May 7 and 8, 2027, his first stop in Toronto since 2022.

The Aperture singer had previously announced a seven-city, three-continent tour, spanning from May to December and including a 30-day residency at New York's Madison Square Garden that he is currently in the middle of. The initial run didn't include any Canadian dates.

Rogers Stadium made headlines recently after it sustained serious damage during a major storm last week, with photos showing sections of the bleachers lying crumpled in the 50,000 capacity outdoor venue.

Live Nation, the operator of the stadium, says sections of the venue will need to be rebuilt before they are safe for use, leading to the cancellation of an AC/DC concert that was set to be the venue's last of the season on Sept. 16.
Presale tickets for Styles's new North American tour dates will be available on Sept. 15, with tickets going on sale officially on Sept. 16.
Rather than carry one or two opening acts with him on each continent of the tour, Styles listed a number of unique supporting acts in an Instagram post Thursday.

Tears for Fears will support Styles at his London dates in the U.K., for instance, while Kylie Minogue is set to appear with Styles in his Los Angeles sets, Tinashe in Phoenix, Caroline Polachek in Paris and Canadian singer Feist in Rome, among others. Toronto's special guest is country singer Lainey Wilson.

According to Live Nation, the tour will be introducing a limited number of $20 tickets (in local currency) for tour dates in North America, as well as £20 tickets and €20 tickets for U.K. and European dates respectively, called "Unpredictable Fun Tickets." Details have not yet been released on when these might be available or how they will be rolled out.

articles.title: Elon Musk calls documentary about him a 'hit piece' after buzzy debut
articles.summary: Elon Musk is reportedly taking legal action against a documentary about him after its buzz-filled debut this week, slamming director Alex Gibney as a "horrible human" on social media.

image.caption: A still from Alex Gibney's Musk, which Elon Musk calls a 'hit piece.' (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Elon Musk is reportedly taking legal action against a documentary about him after its buzz-filled debut this week, slamming director Alex Gibney as a "horrible human" on social media.
Musk is reportedly taking legal action against the production after its Venice Film Festival debut
The world's richest man is the subject of director Gibney's Musk, which debuted at the Venice Film Festival on Tuesday and received a five-minute-long standing ovation.

Critics say the film, which clocks in at nearly four hours, is an incisive look at a man who has built a career as a far-right provocateur and head of a trillion-dollar tech empire through multiple companies, ever-shifting tech promises and aligning himself with powerful figures such as U.S. President Donald Trump.

The Guardian said Tuesday that it was an "epic study of the world's richest and most banal man," while Deadline said it depicted Musk as "petty, narcissistic, megalomaniacal, cruel, detached from humans at a personal level (including various ex-partners and many of his children) while purporting to want to save humanity by colonizing Mars," calling it "the takedown he richly deserves."
Musk will have its Canadian premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sept. 14.
When the documentary was first announced in 2023, Musk called it a "hit piece," a characterization he has repeated multiple times on social media in the past week.

Since Tuesday, Elon Musk has posted a flurry of replies on X agreeing with supporters criticizing the documentary, calling the film "boring," and saying Gibney "lacks integrity" and is a "bitter old man who lost the plot long ago," among other insults.

Musk's attorney Alex Spiro issued a letter to the production, according to The Hollywood Reporter, putting them on formal legal notice and stating that Spiro would proceed with legal action if the production did not "check [their] facts with the people who know them."

Jigsaw Productions issued a statement to The Hollywood Reporter defending the film's accuracy and stating that Musk should be championing the productions' right to examine powerful figures, as "a free speech absolutist."

items: SpaceX stock jumps after record IPO, making Musk the first trillionaire

blocks.text: CBC News reached out to Spiro and Jigsaw Productions, but had not heard back by publication time.
Film tracks childhood to tech empire

Gibney, whose previous films have investigated Scientology, Enron and Casino Jack Abramoff, among other targets, said in Venice before the film's premiere that he believes Musk is "extremely" dangerous to democracy.

It's unclear if Musk has actually seen the film. In the documentary, an AI avatar of Musk mouths along to quotes that Musk has said in the past, an eerie choice that Gibney said was to convey, "the reality of what he's done and the unreality of his narrative."

The film traces Musk's life from his childhood in South Africa to his rise through startups Zip2 and PayPal onto Tesla, SpaceX, Starlink, X and his AI aspirations, while also digging into his alliance with Trump and his chaotic tenure as part of the Department of Government Efficiency, where he helped gut the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) — an action that researchers say has already led to hundreds of thousands of deaths worldwide.
Should Canada crack down on Elon Musk's Grok AI?

The documentary puts its largest focus on Tesla and the company's safety claims related to its self-driving technology, digging into lawsuits and tracking Musk's shifting promises about the capability and safety of the technology across his pursuit of a fully autonomous vehicle.

items: Tesla being investigated after car drives into home, killing 76-year-old woman
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman testifies in high-stakes court bout with Elon Musk
This mom’s son was asking Tesla’s Grok AI chatbot about soccer. It told him to send nude pics, she says

blocks.text: Those interviewed in the documentary include Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard, Musk's first wife Justine Musk, neurologist Sam Harris, tech reporter Kara Swisher and former USAID administrator Samantha Power.
Ashley St. Clair, a former conservative MAGA influencer and former girlfriend of Musk, also appeared in the film. They have one child together, born in 2024.
She joined Gibney at the Venice Film Festival, alleging that she was offered $40 million US to sign a nondisclosure agreement and not speak in the film.
Musk replied to a TMZ report about the alleged NDA, denying that he ever offered her money and claiming she "has a history of making false claims."

The film goes into Musk's takeover of X and what Gibney says is the manipulation of the algorithm. WIRED reporter Zoe Schiffer, who also appears in the film, said at the news conference before the premiere that Musk has "tweaked the algorithm" in favour of "the more inflammatory comments and voices on that platform."
At the same conference, St. Clair said that she believes Musk is stoking fires and "causing deliberate division that could be catastrophic if it's not regulated or contained."
The film will be released in select theatres in North America on Oct. 16., with a wider rollout following on Oct. 23.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca
