articles.title: Former PE teacher faces lengthy jail term for sexually abusing pupils
articles.summary:
Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Wiltshire and Hampshire, and found guilty of charges involving boy

A former PE teacher is facing a lengthy jail sentence…

blocks.text: A former PE teacher is facing a lengthy jail sentence for grooming and sexually abusing three pupils at two schools.
Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Hampshire and Wiltshire and was found guilty by a jury of charges involving a boy.
The Crown Prosecution Service described James’s crimes as “a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care” and praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.

Judge James Bromige asked for reports to be prepared on James so that he could assess the danger she posed when sentencing her later this year. Her defence team said she knew she faced a significant jail sentence.
During her trial at Winchester crown court, jurors were told that James, from Chippenham in Wiltshire, flirted with a 16-year-old boy in class at a school in Southampton.
They began exchanging Snapchat messages and arranged for her to drive him to a promenade, where they kissed in her car.

Later they went to her house where they cuddled while watching the Wimbledon tennis championships on the television before going to her bedroom where they had sex. She told him she loved him and wanted him to move away with her.
Edward Culver, prosecuting, told the trial the school was made aware of the incident after another student showed a teacher some text messages apparently sent between the James and the complainant.

He said: “They suggested a sexually charged relationship. He [the boy] was named as ‘number 8’ in the messages as a cover. She acted not only in an unprofessional and overfamiliar way, but failed to recognise any boundaries, exploiting her position to engage in sexual activity with one of her young students.”
In a police interview, the boy said he had been “groomed” by the defendant.
James was convicted of three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust.

Before the trial, James pleaded guilty to offences against two girls. One was a pupil at the same Southampton school as the boy, the other attended a school in Wiltshire that James had also taught at.
The offences included sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child and making an indecent photograph of a child. The victims were 13 and 14 at the time.

During legal argument, which can now be reported, it also emerged that at the start of her career, James received a warning while she was teaching at the private Seaford college in West Sussex for giving her personal mobile number to a pupil.
Bethany Adams, of the CPS, said: “Bronwen James was trusted to educate and protect children. Instead, she used that trust to groom and sexually abuse three students.
“James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse.
“This was not a lapse in judgment; it was a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care.
“The courage shown by James’s victims in coming forward has been instrumental in securing this conviction. I hope it gives them, and their families, some measure of justice.”

articles.title: Ministers face backlash from industry over plans to allow mayors to impose ‘tourist tax’
articles.summary:
Many mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job losses

Ministers are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they…
articles.byline: Kiran Stacey, Josh Halliday, Alexandra Toppingand Rob Davies

blocks.text: Ministers are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors in England would be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs.

The plan, unveiled on Thursday by Angela Rayner, the local government secretary, will allow mayors to impose a “tourist tax” without a cap on how much they can charge and with few controls on how they can spend it.

The move, which gives mayors some of their most significant tax-raising powers, was welcomed by regional leaders, who said it would give them a vital revenue stream at a time when local government is facing a funding crisis. Mayors will be expected to lay out their detailed plans for how they plan to use the new powers in early 2028.
But it was met with outrage from hospitality businesses, who had expected the government to put stricter conditions on how much mayors could charge and how the money would be used.

UKHospitality, the industry’s trade body, said a 5% overnight levy across England could result in 33,000 job losses and a £2bn hit to the economy, with regions more reliant on tourism, such as the Lake District, being worst affected.

The owner of Premier Inn, Britain’s biggest hotel chain, said it would be “hugely damaging” and urged ministers to “avoid inflicting what could be irreparable harm on this large and vital sector of the economy”.

Eddie Nelder, the co-owner of the five-strong Choice Hotels chain in Blackpool, said: “We’re here trying to stay alive, waiting for a lifeline from the government and we get another hammer blow. It feels like we’re being strangled.”
However, Rayner insisted the tax-raising powers would help fund local communities.
“This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most,” she said in a statement before a meeting with the country’s mayors at No 10 North in Manchester.
“It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.”
In the immediate term, the rate will be set at no more than 5% in almost every major English city after every Labour metro mayor agreed to cap their charges at that level.

In a joint letter to Rayner, they wrote: “Foreign cities visited by British tourists from New York to Paris, as well as hundreds of smaller cities across the world, have long benefited from such levies while continuing to grow their tourism sectors. Granting the power to regions to introduce levies will help level the playing field by ensuring further investment in our cities, contributing to further growth.”
But large parts of the east coast will not have to pay the tax after their mayors – two Reform UK and one Conservative – said they would refuse to impose them.

The move follows a consultation launched by Keir Starmer’s government, and will bring England into line with many European nations and the US, where holidaymakers have for years been paying overnight visitor levies.
Similar levies also apply in Wales and Scotland, though they will be capped in Wales.

Edinburgh became the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax, setting it at 5% in July. In Wales, councils will have the power to charge £1.30 per person a night in tax for most accommodation from April 2027.

Under the proposal, which is expected to be introduced as a bill in parliament within months, mayors will be allowed to charge a levy as a percentage of the price of an overnight stay, rather than as a flat fee.

Ministers at Westminster will cap the number of nights to which it can be applied in order to avoid hitting long-term rental properties. It is understood the cap is likely to be higher than the 5% that is applied by Holyrood.
after newsletter promotion
Any commercially rented property will face the tax, though there will be an exemption for those that are only rented occasionally on a casual basis.
Mayors will be allowed to decide whether or not to exempt other sites such as festival campsites. They will also be allowed to share revenues with local councils.

The move is one of the biggest handovers of power from the Treasury to local leaders in years, and comes before the first budget of Andy Burnham’s government, at which ministers have promised to hand over more tax powers to local leaders.

It comes at a time when many local authorities are struggling for funds. Last year the government gave emergency funding worth £1.3bn to a record 28 councils, without which several said they would have gone bankrupt.

But it also comes after a concerted effort by the government to ease the pressure on the hospitality industry, with many businesses struggling with high inflation and increased national insurance and minimum wage bills.
Earlier this summer, the former chancellor slashed VAT on British summer holiday destinations, in a programme she called the “Great British Summer Savings Scheme”.
Meanwhile, in one of his first acts as prime minister, Burnham announced he would cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
Many hospitality businesses are struggling with high inflation, as well as additional national insurance and minimum wage costs imposed by Reeves in her first budget.

Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “What we’re talking about here is an open-ended power for mayors to set tourism taxes at any level they want … If you go to Paris, if you go to Rome, if you go to Berlin, you’re paying a small tourism tax, but it’s capped.”

articles.title: 'We never recovered him': Quest to identify remains from Ground Zero continues
articles.summary: Since the attacks, New York officials are working with new, complex technology to find traces of more than 1,000 victims.

blocks.text: For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life was his mangled firefighter helmet.

Scauso's father, Dennis - part of a New York City Fire Department (FDNY) hazmat unit for 12 years - initially was not scheduled to work on 11 September, 2001, but switched shifts for the overtime pay.
The Long Island father of four was likely in the South Tower of the World Trade Center when it collapsed, the Scauso family was told. The helmet with his badge number was found months later.
"I've spent essentially my entire life knowing my father died, and learning to live with the fact that we never recovered him," said Scauso, who was four when he died.

Dennis Scauso is one of more than 1,000 people killed on September 11 in New York who have yet to be identified, according to New York City's Office of Chief Medical Examiner. Nearly 3,000 people died in the World Trade Center attacks that day.

Last month, the city announced the identity of a previously unknown victim of the terrorist attacks - the 1,654th person - using a new technology called forensic investigative genetic genealogy - or FIGG.

"There is real promise in using this approach," said Angela Soler, director of forensic anthropology in the city's medical examiner office. "There's hope for more families to receive answers, and hopefully we'll be able to test more remains in the future using this technology as well."
Since 9/11, Soler's office has sought to identify the remains of the 2,753 victims who died in the World Trade Center. So far, 60 percent of those killed have been identified.
"It's been one of the most complex identification efforts that I think anybody has ever really experienced," Soler said.
Efforts to identify victims have been complicated by a number of factors.
Human remains were damaged in the plane crashes and fires caused by jet fuel, meaning the office had only portions of victims for DNA samples, Soler said.

Scauso added that because of the timing of the attacks, many firefighters were changing shifts, but some stayed to help, grabbing whatever extra gear they could find. This meant some first responders recovered were wearing uniforms with others' names, complicating identification.
The World Trade Center site also had many more victims than the other 9/11 terrorist attack sites.

The remains of five of the 184 people killed when American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon were never identified because of similar conditions. According to the National Park Service, enough remains were recovered to use DNA, dental records and fingerprints to identify all 40 victims aboard United Airlines flight 93, which crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

Remains from the World Trade Center have been packaged and sealed to help preserve DNA for testing in the years to come. Soon after the attacks, individuals were identified using fingerprints or dental records, but as time went on, when neither was available, the office turned to DNA. Officials were able to use new technology to extract DNA and retest the same remains.
"That's why all these years down the road, we're still getting new identifications, because we're just continuing to retest and retry with every new technology that becomes available," Soler said.
DNA technology has helped the office identify 1,495 victims since 9/11 - some solely with DNA and others with multiple methods - according to the medical examiner's office.

Last year, the city announced that with the help of DNA, 24 years later, it had identified three new victims - Ryan Fitzgerald, a 26-year-old currency trader, Babara Keating, a 72-year-old who was aboard American Airlines Flight 11 from Boston to Los Angeles, and a woman whose family kept her identity private.

Soler said the new FIGG technology uses whole genome sequencing - which provides a way to read someone's entire genetic code. It means investigators can make more potential matches to family members who are more distant relatives of the victim. Once those matches are made, the New York Police Department helps find relatives who are closer to the victims.
The medical examiner's office in New York still gets weekly calls from loved ones asking about someone whose remains were never recovered.

Many have never been able to bury a loved one, but some families choose to leave the remains - once found - at a repository at the 9/11 memorial site in New York. The repository was built into the bedrock of the World Trade Center site and can only be accessed by medical examiner staff. A nearby private space, known as the reflection room, is available for families to mourn.
"That's where their loved one was in their last moments, and that's where they want them to stay", Soler said.
Some don't want to be notified, perhaps because the confirmation is too painful, said Soler, who helps inform families.

Scauso is one of those people. She knows people who, in recent years, got a call that a relative finally has been identified. The thought of being next on the list is scary for her family, who has worked hard to keep the memory of her father - a jack of all trades and a lover of jazz - alive.

"At this point, an identification wouldn't change the reality of his death. It wouldn't give me back my father, and I don't necessarily want to reopen something that has become part of the way I've learned to live and grieve," she said. "Especially 25 years later, it's going to open up the wounds again."
But, Scauso said, the technology is important.

Soler has seen the news provide a mix of both relief and sadness. "It's confirmation of something that they always knew to be true - they knew their loved one died on 9/11, but I think for many families, there's still that question in the back of their mind until the remains are formally identified," Soler said.
"Maybe they're reliving it a little bit more now, having this new identification. But at the same time, it closes one chapter of their journey after 9/11," she added.

To Soler - and some of her current colleagues who also were on the ground during 9/11 - the work is deeply personal. Workers from their office arrived at Ground Zero after the planes hit the towers, and were there when the buildings collapsed.
They are aware it is unlikely they will identify every victim of the New York attacks. In some instances, there may be no remains of a victim at all. Still, they have no plans to stop.
"As long as there's families looking for answers, we'll continue searching for them," she said.

articles.title: Poilievre tells U.S. TV Canadians are 'wounded' and 'confused' to be in America's crosshairs
articles.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is telling Americans their northern neighbours are feeling "wounded" and "confused" over how Canada and its economy became a key target for U.S. President Donald…

image.caption: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, shown here speaking in Windsor, Ont., is in New York to speak directly to Americans about how free trade can lift both countries. (Dax Melmer/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is telling Americans their northern neighbours are feeling "wounded" and "confused" over how Canada and its economy became a key target for U.S. President Donald Trump.
'I'm not going to attack my prime minister on foreign soil,' Conservative leader says
"I think we feel a little bit wounded," Poilievre told reporters on the U.S. network CNBC on Thursday during a trip to New York where he is advocating for a return to normal trade relations.
"We're kind of confused as to how it is, suddenly, that Canada ended up in the crosshair."

The Conservative leader said Canada and the U.S. have a deeply interconnected economic relationship that has delivered peace and prosperity for decades and the only way forward should be tariff-free trade.

"Both countries are going to have their grievances," he said. "America had buy-America policies that prevented us from selling into subnational procurement markets and tariffs on our softwood lumber.… But the bottom line is: let's sit down and work them out for the mutual benefit of our people."
In a statement Poilievre said he went to New York to fight against tariffs and for jobs on both sides of the border.

He said he will be meeting with investors and business leaders but his "main audience is the American people" to which he is making the case "that both our countries can be safer, richer and more affordable if we trade freely."
Poilievre also said he will stay in New York for the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, to honour the victims and highlight "how Canadians and Americans stood together after the terrorist attacks."
'Politics ends at the border': Poilievre

That national spirit was on display during Poilievre's CNBC interview, when he refused to be goaded into answering a question about whether he believed Prime Minister Mark Carney was acting in good faith during the recent round of trade negotiations.

"I'm not going to attack my prime minister on foreign soil. It's just not something I'm going to do," he said. "My mission here is to fight for my country, not to score political points domestically. Politics ends at the border."
Poilievre said Canada needs to leverage the "single biggest asset Canada has in the U.S., which is our friendship with the American people who overwhelmingly love Canada."
Co-host Joe Kernen said he respected Poilievre for refusing to criticize Carney while abroad, noting that politicians in opposition in the U.S. do not maintain that standard.
"You actually have a little bit of class," Kernen said.

items: What will Trump's retaliatory tariffs do to Canada’s economy big picture? Not that much, economists predict
'Unhinged' for Canada to call dispute with U.S. a trade war, says Trump's tariff chief
Trade war, Alberta referendum loom large as Carney charts cabinet's year forward

blocks.text: When Kernen pressed Poilievre on Canada's economic performance over the last decade, the Conservative leader also avoided criticizing the country, saying Canada has had "a lot of good public policy successes by different levels of government."

Going forward Poilievre said rivals and risks to the U.S. are "slowly mounting" and rather than combat them on their own, the U.S. should rebuild the Western alliance that won the Cold War rather than fighting with friends.
"I think the United States would be better off if it united with those countries that believe in free speech, free markets, free trade and free people," he said.
"We could build an incredible North American fortress with the resources that we have on this continent, but it's going to take a collaborative relationship to do it."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.

articles.title: Yemen: Houthis take control of strategic Red Sea port city
articles.summary: The Houthi takeover of Mokha comes amid intensified fighting that has sparked fears of a return to civil war. The Red Sea has served as a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz amid the US war with…

image.caption: The port city of Mokha lies near the crucial Bab el-Mandeb strait [FILE: August 10, 2026]Image: Al Joumhouriya TV/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Yemen's Houthi militia captured the port city of Mokha (also spelled Mocha) on Thursday, sparking fears the country could return to civil war.
The city lies around 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the Bab el-Mandeb strait, an important waterway for shipping that divides the Red Sea from the Gulf of Aden.
The Red Sea has served as a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted amid the United States' war with Iran, sending global oil prices skyrocketing.

Houthi spokesperson Abdulsalam was cited by the Reuters news agency as saying that freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the Strait remain safe and operations are limited to specific targets.
The Houthis have in the past targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, saying it is in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza.
Meanwhile, Houthi rebels accused Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on the southwestern province of Taiz.
"The Saudi enemy launched 10 strikes on the Dhubab district in western Taiz," the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel was cited by AFP news agency as saying.
Dhubab lies just south of Mokha.
Fighting intensifies between Houthis and Yemeni government

Fighting has intensified between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government in recent months after four years of relative calm, with rebels intensifying efforts to solidify their control over the country's coastline.
The capture of Mokha is the Iran-backed militia's biggest territorial gain since a UN-brokered truce signed in 2022.
The Iran-backed Houthis control the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, as well as much of the more populous areas in the country's north and west.
The internationally recognized government has its headquarters in the southern city of Aden and receives considerable support from Saudi Arabia.
Yemen's civil war has killed over 150,000 people and brought others to the brink of famine.

articles.title: Cyberattack in Berlin: 1.4 million files on the Dark Web
articles.summary: Shortly before Berlin's state parliamentary election, the hacker group Rhysida stole data, tried to extort the Berlin Senate and published the data on the dark web after their attempt failed.

image.caption: After a failed extortion attempt, hackers published 1.4 million records from the Berlin administrationImage: picture alliance/dpa

blocks.text: It was a story that almost went unnoticed amid all the clamor surrounding the closely watched state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. This highly alarming story is one of many recent reports that have detailed attacks on infrastructure or drone attacks on airports carried out by hostile foreign powers. Incidents like this one in the German capital highlight just how vulnerable Germany's data networks are.

So what exactly happened? Since early September, employee files, official correspondence, pay stubs, and even scanned ID documents have been appearing on the dark web. The hacker group Rhysida stole the data and then tried to extort the Berlin city government. They demanded a ransom of 30 bitcoins, which is equivalent to about €2 million ($2.3 million), or else they would publish the sensitive data.

But last Friday, Berlin's Governing Mayor Kai Wegner stated: "The State of Berlin will not give in to blackmail." The data was subsequently published on the dark web, the part of the internet accessible only to tech-savvy users. In total, the data set consists of approximately 1.4 million records.
Explained: How Germany will expand intel powers, and why
An employee unknowingly opened a phishing email

Two departments of the city government serving approximately four million residents have been compromised: the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transportation. This time, the attack wasn't carried out by foreign intelligence agencies, but by criminals.

The hackers initially gained access to protected data between August 7 and 14 without being detected. Rhysida, a cybercrime group believed to originate from Eastern Europe, has been attacking public institutions around the world since 2023, claiming responsibility for nearly 280 attacks, primarily in the US.

The hackers were able to gain access when a Berlin Transportation Authority employee replied to a phishing email, a message disguised to appear genuine and benign. Opening one of the attachments inadvertently grants the attackers access to the victim's network.
In Berlin, the state government's secure fiber-optic network connects approximately 600 locations, ranging from municipal offices to senate departments.
Data disclosure could have serious consequences

The list of sectors that experts believe could be compromised illustrates the real gravity of the data breach. In addition to the personal data of employees and citizens, this includes information on combi-heat and power plants, fuel storage facilities, emergency power supply systems as well as prisons and water treatment plants.

In an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine Newspaper, Jochim Selzer of the Chaos Computer Club said that the publication could have serious consequences for the people affected — even if the data only appeared on the hard-to-access dark web: "The more you know about a person, the better you can impersonate them and the better you can figure out what you need to know about them in order to, say, place an order on their behalf."
As cyberattacks threaten Germany, can Berlin keep data safe?
Is changing passwords enough?

And what about the political authorities responsible? The Berlin state government has instructed its employees to change their passwords. That, however, sparked outrage from Thorsten Schleheider, the vice-chairman of Berlin's police union. He said that Berlin's data has been inadequately protected for years and that many employees have not received sufficient training: "It is unthinkable that highly sensitive data was compromised for days, and the only action taken appears to be instructing employees to change their passwords."

To address the data breach, the Berlin Senate has set up a coordination office involving all Berlin administrative agencies. It has also established contact with federal agencies such as the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), based in Bonn. Mayor Kai Wegner said, "We will inform, advise and support those employees and Berliners who were affected as quickly as possible."
Berlin state elections on September 20 remain safe

The Berlin authorities were, however, able to provide reassurance regarding at least one issue of concern. They announced that the September 20 election for the Berlin State Parliament is not at risk. State Election Commissioner Stephan Bröchler told the Bild newspaper: "As things stand, all systems and processes necessary for the election remain unaffected — including election preparations, the actual election day itself and the steps leading up to the release of the preliminary results."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was at least indirectly affected by the data theft. The stolen information also includes details about the controversial expansion of the Chancellery in the heart of Berlin.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
articles.summary: Analysts question if the US president's election year offer is workable, legal or affordable.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
US President Donald Trump has offered every adult American $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win November's midterm elections, but it is unclear how such a plan would be funded and whether it is legal.
His remarks prompted raucous applause from supporters at a party convention on Wednesday night, but Democrats labelled it an "empty promise".
Trump also told the Republican conference that the money would have to be spent in the US, but it is unclear how that would be monitored.

The US president has given no details on how it would be funded, though Vice-President JD Vance suggested it might be paid for by tariff revenue and that such cheques would not go to wealthy Americans.
Is Trump's offer legal?
Under US federal law, it is illegal to give payments that are intended to influence the way a person is voting.
However, some experts have said the offer made by Trump in Texas on Wednesday could be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal.

Dr Joan Mahoney, lecturer in law at the University of Southampton, told the BBC she thought the offer would be legal as it would be similar to a campaign promise - though she said politicians "don't usually do it quite this explicitly".
"On the one hand it sounds a bit like a bribe, vote for the Republicans and you'll get money, which would be decidedly illegal," she said.
"But on the other hand it would go to everyone, regardless of how they voted so it isn't in that sense a bribe.
"I think it would be legal. It's the same kind of campaign pledge as saying 'if my party wins we'll reduce taxes'. Every party does that all the time... and that's obviously perfectly legal."

However, Laurel Rapp, director of the US and North America programme at Chatham House, told the BBC that Trump's offer seemed to be "a very different, very transactional agreement" from the kind of promise usually made by candidates in an election period.
Watch: BBC North America editor Sarah Smith looks into whether Trump's promise stands up
How much would it cost?
Aside from the question of legality, some have also asked whether Trump's offer would be feasible financially in the context of increasing US debt, partially as a result of the war in Iran.
There are nearly 270 million American adults, meaning a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.
Trump gave no details on how such cheques would be funded.
Congress authorises spending in the US, but the president did not say whether he planned to ask for legislative approval for any payments.
And legal experts said it was unlikely he could approve such a vast sum via a presidential executive order.
Erica York, a senior economist at the Washington DC-based Tax Foundation, told the BBC she would be "extremely surprised" if Congress approved any proposal.
"This would be one of the worst ways to use $1.3 trillion," she said.
"We're on a very unsustainable track, with deficits only projected to grow and grow," York added.
Could tariff revenue fund it?
Speaking to Fox News after Trump's speech, Vice-President Vance indicated that the payments could be funded by money raised by the president from tariffs.
However, such revenue to date falls far short of the money that would be needed to account for Trump's $5,000 cheques offer.
According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the US has brought in around $475bn in tariff and excise tax revenue since the beginning of 2025.
But more than $100bn has been refunded after the Supreme Court struck down many tariffs earlier this year.
When asked how the payouts could work, the White House said in a statement to the BBC: "The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump."
"With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results," added spokesman Davis Ingle.
Why has Trump made the offer?
One former Republican strategist and pollster said Trump's latest offer should be firmly seen in the context of an election that is now less than two months away.
"It is an extraordinary promise, and I'm not sure where that money is going to come from - but it is campaign season," Robert Moran told the BBC.
Chatham House's Rapp said Trump was thinking short term to try to keep hold of Congress as he enters the final two years of his term in office.
"Money is something that he is now resorting to because the polling is not looking good for Republicans and the polling is not looking good for him," she continued.
Has anything similar happened before?
Trump has previously proposed $2,000 cheques to be funded by tariff revenues, but those payouts have not materialised.
Former President Joe Biden was accused of buying votes when he promised $2,000 Covid stimulus cheques for Americans if Democrats won Senate elections in Georgia in January 2021.

A similar controversy arose ahead of the 2024 presidential election, during which billionaire Trump supporter Elon Musk offered cash incentives to registered voters in seven swing states who signed a certain petition.
Additional reporting by Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter

articles.title: August was Earth's hottest month, European climate agency finds
articles.summary: Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August, blowing far past a key climate threshold due to the dangerous double whammy of human-caused climate change and a supersized El Niño, according…

image.caption: People cool off near the Colosseum in Rome during a heat wave in early August. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)

blocks.text: Science·New

Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August, blowing far past a key climate threshold due to the dangerous double whammy of human-caused climate change and a supersized El Niño, according to the European climate service Copernicus.
'This is the spiralling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction,' says UN's climate chief
August's sizzle also helped push the globe and Canada to swelter through the hottest Northern Hemisphere summer scientists have measured.

Last month the world averaged 16.96 C, which technically was one-hundredth of a degree Celsius more than the all-time global mark set in July 2023. But because that's also the uncertainty level, it's considered a tie, said Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus.

"It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago," Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler said in an email.
"The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we're going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over."

Globally, August was 1.65 C above pre-industrial levels, far exceeding the longer term 1.5 C threshold set by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. The eight hottest months on record have all been from July 2023 on, according to Copernicus data.
"Our climate system is really operating well outside the range we would have expected just a decade ago," Burgess said Wednesday from a United Kingdom that has been beset with heat waves.
Millions across Europe facing record temperatures from major heat wave

"We've transitioned from climate being very abstract and perhaps impacting the Global South or faraway places to climate impacting and disrupting our daily lives with schools closing, hospitals being overwhelmed, roads melting, train lines buckling. And the reality is we will get more of these conditions that we've seen this summer."

Global monthly ocean temperatures in August tied a March 2024 all-time record for the warmest month recorded, while Aug. 22 set a record for the hottest day recorded in the world's seas, according to Copernicus.
An extra-hot summer hits
"This summer has really been exceptional. We've seen records that existed for close to 100 years be broken, in the U.S. in particular," Burgess said.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on Wednesday announced that for the first time, summer in the lower 48 states was hotter than during the peak of the devastating Dust Bowl in 1936.

Until humanity stops burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records, killing millions and costing trillions.- United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell

June through August of 2026 in the contiguous United States averaged 23.54 C, nearly four-tenths of a degree warmer than the mark set 90 years earlier. Globally, this past summer also tied with 2024 for the hottest on record, according to Copernicus.

That records are regularly getting broken, and that August and not July — which is traditionally warmer — set an all-time record, are signs that human-caused climate change is accelerating, Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather said.

items: Heat dome brings dangerous temperatures. Here's how to stay safe
Record-breaking heat dome growing to cover nearly the entire U.S.

blocks.text: Fossil fuels, El Niño blamed

Several scientists said while El Niño is a factor, this natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps and warms weather globally is nowhere as big a cause as the heat-trapping gases emitted as humans burn coal, oil and natural gas.

"While El Niño is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Niño hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas, these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming," said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London.
Burgess said El Niño generally adds only one- or two-tenths of a degree Celsius to the global temperature with the overwhelming rest of the heat coming from the burning of fossil fuels.
France records 1,000 additional deaths amid record breaking heat wave

This El Niño is forecast, however, to break records for strength in the coming months. And as temperatures continue to rise, heat waves, storms, floods and wildfires will get more frequent and more dangerous, said Texas Tech climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe.

According to Hausfather, "it is increasingly likely that 2026 ends up beating 2024 as the warmest year on record, and almost certain that 2027 beats both, potentially reaching as high as 1.8 C above pre-industrial levels on the back of an unprecedentedly-strong El Niño event."
Some days may hit an even higher climate threshold: 2 C above mid-1800s, Burgess said.

items: Canadians should prepare for a 5 C hotter future, report warns

blocks.text: "Until humanity stops burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records, killing millions and costing trillions, hitting transport and health systems, and pushing up prices for household basics like food," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said.
"This is the spiralling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling."

articles.title: Separatists dominating Alberta referendum conversation online: report
articles.summary: Debate about Alberta independence is dominated by a loose network of citizens, advocates and anonymous social media accounts. Some of whom are also selling home decor.

image.caption: Debate about Alberta independence is dominated by a loose network of citizens, advocates and anonymous social media accounts. (Joel Dryden/CBC)

blocks.text: On the morning of Alberta Day this year, also known as the first of September, one of the most influential separatist social media accounts in the province sprung into action to mark the occasion.

The anonymous account known as Rise of Alberta, which has amassed almost 100,000 followers on X with a consistent flow of independence content, began the day with a dramatically backlit Alberta flag to celebrate the province’s future as a “free and independent country.”

Then came a clip of Premier Danielle Smith talking about the referendum, a shot of a celebratory Alberta Day drone show against a dark sky, and, finally, a link to a site where you could buy a “classic, handcrafted” Alberta flag blanket that comes in a variety of sizes and starts at $75. (They are made, the site notes, in the U.S.)

According to a new analysis from the Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy's Media Ecosystem Observatory, co-led by McGill University and the University of Toronto, the account is the most influential player in the raging online debate about Alberta independence that is dominated by a loose network of grassroots citizens, passionate advocates and anonymous social media accounts. Some of whom are also selling home decor.

“I think this is, in many ways, what modern political campaigns look like,” says Chris Ross, a senior analyst with the Observatory, pointing to the increasingly blurred lines between social media influencing, commerce and regular old politics.
“The general public needs to wrap our heads around this and think, ‘OK, this is becoming more normal, so how should we think about this?’” Ross added.
“And should we be giving it more scrutiny?”

Unlike in, say, Quebec, there is no elected party campaigning for sovereignty in Alberta, which has left the campaign for independence largely in the hands of a leaderless group of individuals with a wide range of beliefs and allegiances.
Passionate network
Online, the study suggests this has manifested as a passionate network of influencers, memes and online spaces devoted to the cause.

The analysis, released Thursday, paints a picture of an online conversation dominated by the separatists, in contrast to real world polling which suggests that support for independence has remained consistent at roughly a quarter of the population.

Among those with the biggest sway identified in the report, the pro-independence influencers outnumber their critics almost two to one, and receive roughly eight times as many likes, comments and shares.

In order to capture the online conversation, researchers collected all the posts on five social media platforms — Instagram, X, YouTube, TikTok and Bluesky — that included the word “Alberta,” plus related terms such as “referendum,” “sovereignty,” and “separatist.” (Facebook was not included because the site does not allow the search of specific terms in the same way.)
They then screened-out the accounts of politicians and media organizations, as well as those that fell below a certain threshold for engagement.

The result was 114 political influencers that were responsible for roughly half of the total social media engagement on this topic since the beginning of 2025. The report names the 40 most significant accounts, defined as those with more than 50,000 engagements on the posts collected as part of the study.

“The independence movement is, obviously, not a fan of Canada’s federal institutions, so I think modern technology allows for this guerrilla-style campaign strategy that really does end up in front of people’s eyes on their feeds,” Ross said.

The account driving the most engagement was Rise Of Alberta, whose posts on X have received over two million engagements over the last year and a half. (There was no response to the requests for comment that CBC News sent to the Rise Of Alberta accounts on X and Facebook.)

The top seven accounts are all similarly pro-independence, and include the personal accounts of notable figures in the movement, such as Keith Wilson, head of the Alberta Transition Council, and Jeffrey Rath, spokesperson for the Alberta Prosperity Society.

But the list also includes an account called Tablesalt, which has recently posted about everything from tariffs to home invasions to criticism of Jason Kenney, while misteristersunshinebaby, which describes itself as “born in Canada before it became the 51st state,” is ninth.

The most influential federalist account belongs to Thomas Lukaszuk, the founder of the Forever Canadian petition, which ranks eighth, with just over 181,000 interactions since the beginning of 2025. The account of former premier Jason Kenney, who has become a very public defender of confederation, ranks 32nd.

Chatter about Alberta separation of any kind is an outsize driver of online engagement, Ross noted. “There is just something about the spectacle of a province potentially leaving Canada that is naturally very interesting,” he said. “It’s like rubbernecking at a car accident.”
But the separatists have emotion on their side, he noted, as they appeal to the anger and fear that many of their followers feel about Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa.

Social media influencers have become a major source of political information more broadly in Canada, Ross points out, and some users have also come to prefer the more conversational tone of the separatist camp, compared to the missives from mainstream government or political institutions, who tend to lean federalist.
“There’s something deep in the human brain that likes seeing these off-the-cuff takes more,” he said.
Piggybacking on COVID

Another big part of the pro-separatists’ success is that they didn’t have to build their network from scratch, says Jean-Christophe Boucher, an associate professor of political science at the University of Calgary.

The independence influencers “piggyback on a network that was built, at least since COVID,” says Boucher, who was not involved in the writing of the report but has worked in monitoring online influence campaigns.

Some of the influencers on the list were also active during the trucker convoy in Ottawa and during the contested ostrich cull in British Columbia, he says, both of which were magnets for activists concerned about what they saw as government overreach.

“That capacity to already have an audience, to have people excited and engaged on these issues is a huge benefit for them,” Boucher said. “Whereas the federalist camp has to build everything from scratch.”

While the data isn’t clear on whether online posts have the ability to influence what people believe, Boucher argues that the dominance of separatist content online has the potential to affect mobilization and voter turnout.
“It gives the pro-separatist camp the perception, a false perception, that they’re mobilized,” Boucher said. “The odds that they will go vote will increase… because they think they’re winning.”

articles.title: Pilot warned Amazon cargo plane going too fast before deadly crash, data shows
articles.summary: One pilot told the other about the aircraft's "excessive speed" but received an uneven response even as alarms sounded.

blocks.text: The flight data released by NTSB included the plane's speed, altitude, and other details like flap deployment as it approached the runway. The update also included the summary of conversation between the two pilots.
The summary noted the pilot's cautions about speed occurred "throughout the remainder of the recording" as did the inconsistent verbal response.
The update said there was an electronic "sink rate sink rate" callout during the final minutes - an automated safety warning about the speed of descent.
There was also an ​electronic "too low terrain" callout, another automated verbal warning that the plane was flying too close to the ground without being properly prepared for landing.

Aviation attorney Pablo Rojas told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that it was difficult to know without the actual recording what the NTSB was referring to when it noted the inconsistent verbal response.
"But, it really confirms that this was, in a way, a doomed approach," he said.

Rojas noted that flap deployment data included in NTSB's update also could be an area of concern. The flaps, located on the back of the wings, are "part of what helps the plane kind of slow down and gently approach a landing", he said.
"The flap deployment here happened much later in the accident sequence," Rojas said. "That's maybe because the pilots were responding to the fact that they were going too fast."
After it overshot the runway, the plane - Amazon Prime Air Flight 7598 - struck equipment on the ground, hit a white Ford van, then continued onward through a perimeter fence.
It then collided with a Toyota Corolla, before coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.

The five who died were part of a plane-cleaning crew in the van. Miami authorities on Tuesday identified them as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

articles.title: More than 20 children feared dead in DR Congo school fire
articles.summary: Officials say there was a stampede as they fled a fire that engulfed two schools in the eastern rebel-held city of Bukavu.

blocks.text: At least 24 schoolchildren are feared dead in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, a senior official there has said.
Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.
Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.
Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.
Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.
A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.
Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.
Rebel‑appointed authorities say they are assessing the situation and will release a provisional death toll this evening.
Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.
"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.

"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."
The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.
In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

articles.title: Germany’s Goethe-Institut is closing in Russia. Russians tell DW how canceled exams are upending their plans
articles.summary: Canceled language exams, disrupted plans to study in Germany and the disappearance of an important cultural link: DW users shared how the closure of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia affects their…

image.caption: The Goethe-Institut in Moscow is one of three branches of Germany’s cultural center that'll have to closeImage: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Germany's Goethe-Institut will close all Russian branches by September 13 amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.

The Russian foreign ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens.

"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Secretary General of the Goethe-Institut Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."

blocks.caption: The library of the Goethe-Institut's Moscow branch won't be accessible anymore after September 13 eitherImage: Timur Gusarov/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.
'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams

Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.
Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.

"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.
DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.
"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig

It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.
Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard

The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.

"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.
"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.
"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.

Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.
'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'
Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.

"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."

blocks.caption: Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany was the target of an attempted drone attack in August 2026Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.

"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.
Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.

"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.
Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship
Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.
"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.

A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.
President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."
According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

articles.title: NBI tapped to probe woman’s death after plastic surgery
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) was tapped to look into the death of a woman who supposedly died after undergoing plastic surgery procedures performed by a celebrity…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) was tapped to look into the death of a woman who supposedly died after undergoing plastic surgery procedures performed by a celebrity plastic surgeon in San Juan City.

The woman’s son, Ronn Tristan Perez, who is a Filipino-American reality television star based in the United States, arrived at the NBI’s Homicide Division on Thursday to seek the investigation into the death of his mother.
In an interview with reporters, Perez said his mother underwent four cosmetic procedures — such as liposuction, Brazilian butt lift, tummy tuck, and body tite for arms — on March 2.
He said these procedures cost P570,000 and were performed by the celebrity surgeon for seven hours.

“Just a quick Google search of it, those are the most dangerous things that you can perform. So you should do due diligence before you even do it. And then even extra care while you’re doing it. And extra care afterwards. That’s like common knowledge,” Perez said.
“And so I’m hoping that all of that was taken into consideration. That people weren’t just taking her money, preying on her insecurities about her looks and making a quick buck off of her,” he added.
According to Perez, his mother started becoming pale after undergoing the four plastic surgery procedures at the celebrity surgeon’s clinic.
“I FaceTime her, and she’s pale, she’s missing a tooth. I said, ‘What’s happening, Mom?’ Me and my brother were both worried,” Perez said.
“Next thing I know, 3 a.m., a couple of days later, I get a phone call from my uncle and my dad, and it was my mom dead.”
Perez claimed he asked the clinic for his mother’s medical records but did not receive all of the documents he wanted to see.

“I’m not accusing anyone of anything. I need more than that. I need documents, papers, expertise that what was done here is everything that was supposed to be done. No stones left unturned,” said Perez.
The NBI is currently looking into the matter. /das

articles.title: Safer infrastructure, water security sought
articles.summary: A private sector body that advises President Marcos on government policies is pushing for measures that seek to make buildings safer, as well as manage floods and ensure water security, citing the…

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 12:00am

With regard to flooding, the council suggested the clearing of the Manggahan Floodway, pursuing the Parañaque Spillway, supporting waste-to-energy facilities and creating a Department of Water Resources to ensure better coordination of flood control, drainage, drought response and water supply.
The Philippine STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — A private sector body that advises President Marcos on government policies is pushing for measures that seek to make buildings safer, as well as manage floods and ensure water security, citing the need for faster and more coordinated action to mitigate the impact of disasters.
The Private Sector Advisory Council (PSAC) presented its recommendations during its eighth infrastructure sector meeting with President Marcos at Malacañang yesterday.

The meeting tackled concrete measures to strengthen the country’s infrastructure resilience and water security, enforce higher standards for buildings and construction materials and improve disaster preparedness, flood management and water infrastructure, according to the Presidential Communications Office.
“We should not wait for the next earthquake, flood or drought. We need to act before it happens,” Sabin Aboitiz, PSAC lead convenor and president of Aboitiz Equity Ventures, said yesterday.

To ensure the safety of buildings, the council is calling for the full implementation of PNS 49:2026 or stronger standards for earthquake-resistant reinforcing steel and tighter checks on imported cement.
PSAC is also seeking a Building Resilience Seal for homes and buildings inspected and found to be resilient to earthquakes.

Noting that 12,500 metric tons of imported cement were destroyed by the trade department last April for failing key strength and durability tests, the group called for strict enforcement of required testing before such products reach the market.

Meanwhile, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon said that all major national roads and highways will have street drainage inlets and built-in trash traps to standardize flood-resistant road infrastructure throughout the country, starting with Metro Manila.

Dizon said the policy for a nationwide widening of street drainage inlets and the integration of built-in trash traps came after successful tests along EDSA by the Department of Public Works and Highways. – Rainier Allan Ronda
