articles.title: Uganda: Traditional kingdom plunged into succession crisis
articles.summary: A royal succession committee and the family of late King Oyo Nyimba of Toroo have put forward competing candidates. Questions have been raised as to whether the late monarch indeed had a son as his…

image.caption: Oyo Nyimba (center) at his official coronation in 2010Image: Samuel Egadu/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: Uganda's traditional kingdom of Tooro has been plunged into a sucession crisis after the family of late monarch Oyo Nyimba rejected on Thursday other clan members' choice of successor.
Although Uganda is a republic, it contains several ancient kingdoms whose leaders are still held in high regard as keepers of tradition and maintain significant social influence.

Oyo, who was also known by his regnal name Rukidi IV, became the world's youngest monarch at the age of three in 1995 following the death of his father. His ascension celebrations were attended by longtime Ugandan strongman President Yoweri Museveni.
His reign was overseen by a series of relatives acting as regents until he turned 18 in 2010.
He died on August 27 at the age of 34 while undergoing cancer treatment in the United States.
Who are the main players in the succession fight?
On Wednesday, the royal clan's succession committee named the late king's cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as the next monarch.
Kijanangoma is a television anchor at public broadcaster UBC.
However, Oyo's mother and sister announced on Thursday that they rejected this proposal, indicating that the king had left a will declaring his son his successor.
His mother Queen Kemigisa called the committee a "self-appointed group of clan members" who had named a new king despite knowing the contents of Oyo's will.
She also accused the Ugandan military of placing her family under house arrest.

The identity of Oyo's son and the son's mother remains a mystery. A campaigner for HIV/AIDS prevention and environmental causes, he had not publicly acknowledged a son until Toroo's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki announced the boy's existence after Oyo's death.

The controversy grew after Andrew Mwenda, a well-known journalist and relative of Oyo's, wrote on social media site X that a son could only succeed a father in Toroo if he was born to a queen, and said that the family had not produced so much as a picture of the boy.

Prime Minister Armstrong called for both sides to remain calm on Thursday, saying the process "should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our King still awaits burial."
Oyo's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

articles.title: How Celine Dion became a pop culture icon across generations
articles.summary: As the global star kicks off her anticipated Paris residency, here's how Celine Dion managed to gain younger followers, while keeping her loyal older fans.

image.caption: In recent years, she's renewed her image by opting for more expressive fashionImage: Martin Harris/Captital Pictures/picture alliance

blocks.text: On September 12, Celine Dion kicks off a series of 26 sold-out concerts, part of a Paris residency held through May 2027. Some 500,000 people are expected to attend the performances, marking the global star's highly anticipated return to the stage following a prolonged break.
In 2022, she announced that she was battling with a rare and incurable neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome. The health issues led her to cancel her world tour.
In the summer of 2024, she returned to the spotlight atop the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics, her resilience giving hope to fans worldwide.

Now, in the days ahead of her Paris concerts, Dion has been thrilling hundreds of fans gathered in front of her hotel, taking the time to chat with them for a few minutes every day, sometimes even joining them in spontaneous sing-alongs and dances.

blocks.caption: Charming her fans with candid moments at the Royal Monceau Hotel in ParisImage: Cyril Pecquenard/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The best-selling Canadian artist of all time, Dion has released a total of 27 studio albums, sold more than 200 million records worldwide and earned multiple Grammy Awards.
Even though her most defining hits date back to the 1990s, she is more than a nostalgia act, as her appeal is now skyrocketing with Gen Z and millennial listeners.
How did that happen?

blocks.caption: 'It's All Coming Back to Me Now': Her power ballads are surging in popularity againImage: Joel Goodman/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A modern fashion darling

In her daily exchanges with her fans on her way to rehearsals, she's always wearing fresh couture pieces: an asymmetrical Loewe gown, a bold blue Givenchy leather dress by Sarah Burton or a striking jacket by Tom Ford.
"Celine Dion is turning the streets of Paris into her runway," wrote Vogue magazine in reaction to her stylish outfits.

"She's always really been into fashion, already in the 1990s, even though we long didn't know this," says Quebec cultural reporter Stephane Leclair, author and host of a podcast series on the star's "D'eux" album. "You know, Celine Dion was never considered 'cool.' She's always had that slightly corny, slightly goofy side. But through her genuine interest for fashion, she’s managed to revamp her image quite a bit."

A notable move came in 2016: Dion admired Zendaya's edgy red carpet looks so much that she tracked down her stylist, Law Roach, and asked him to team up with her. She credits Roach with transforming her into a modern fashion darling.
But that's just one aspect that explains her ongoing — and renewed — popularity.
A rags to riches story

Born on March 30, 1968, Celine Dion was the youngest of 14 children of a poor family in French-speaking in Quebec, Canada. As she proudly notes on her official website, the house was so full that, as a baby, she had to sleep in a drawer instead of a crib.

She grew up surrounded by music, and recorded her first song at the age of 12. It impressed music manager René Angélil so much that he mortgaged his house to pay for her first record. She quickly emerged as a child star in Quebec.

blocks.caption: Her winning performance at the Eurovision Song Contest in 1988Image: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Inspired by Michael Jackson, she decided that she wanted to become a megastar. She won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 1988 and launched her first English-language album, "Unison," in 1990.
This, however, sparked cultural tension among French-speaking fans in Quebec, who felt she was neglecting her roots to pursue American and international superstardom.

"We were between two referendums on Quebec's independence at the time," points out Leclair. But even after she became a global star, she proudly kept identifying as the "little girl from Charlemagne," the small town near Montreal where she grew up.
"People in Quebec quickly understood that it didn't change anything, that she would always remain one of them, and that it only added another layer to her career," notes the cultural reporter.

Indeed, she also kept working in French all while building her career as a global pop artist. Teaming up with popular French song-writer Jean-Jacques Goldman, they released "D'eux" in 1995. It became the best-selling French-language album of all time.

The theme song for "Beauty and the Beast" (1991) won her both a Grammy and an Academy Award, while her best-selling "My Heart Will Go On" (1997) for the blockbuster film "Titanic" cemented her status alongside music's greatest vocalists.
Adding groundbreaking edge to Las Vegas

While other aging stars would head to the Las Vegas Strip to finish their careers, Dion revolutionized the music industry with "A New Day...," her high-profile residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace: With a total of 714 performances from 2003 to 2007, she demonstrated how such residencies could be modern, cutting-edge — and extremely lucrative.
It served as a blueprint for Las Vegas residencies by younger stars, such as Britney Spears and Adele.
Viral authenticity

"The world's biggest stars are often dead set on protecting a perfect, untouchable image. Celine, on the other hand, is incredibly accessible. She isn't afraid to let her true, authentic personality shine through," points out Leclair.
"And Celine's die-hard fans just love her humorous side," he adds. "They love the fact that she's a bit wacky. It makes her really relatable."

Famous for spontaneously breaking into song during interviews, those moments, as well as various over-the-top scenes from her 1990s music videos, have been picked up in Internet memes and TikTok trends.

Encouraged by her teenage sons, she launched her own official TikTok account in January 2026. She went viral with a "What's in My Bag?" video where she pulls out a mix of everyday essentials and completely unhinged items.
Writing a new chapter
But beyond the humor, she's also ready to share her most vulnerable moments.
In 2016, she lost her husband — her manager, René Angélil — and a brother to cancer within the same week. Her 2019 album "Courage" focused on loss and recovery.

blocks.caption: Their 26-year age gap and the fact that Dion was only 12 when she met her manager and future husband made headlines, but they stayed together until his deathImage: Ryan Remiorz/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Her 2024 documentary "I am: Celine Dion," in which she looks back on her life and career all while addressing how she deals with her stiff-person syndrome diagnosis, has been praised by critics as intensely sincere and visceral.

One scene of the film follows her as she suffers from a painful spasm: "I don't think many stars of that caliber would have agreed to be filmed — and have the footage included in the final cut — in such an unflattering state," notes Leclair. "It was partly out of a desire for transparency, to explain to her fans why she had to step back."
And her fans highly value this authenticity, as well as her resilience.

She is now undergoing physical and therapies to manage her symptoms and be able to perform again for this series of more than 2-hour-long concerts. They will feature 18 musicians and four backing singers; a live choir will also join them on stage for several songs.

Additionally, Paris will mark the start of the concert series with two giant karaoke sessions on September 11. A total of 10,000 people are expected to take part in the participatory event celebrating her four decades of songs.

articles.title: Man 27, charged in stabbing inside Edmonton Sikh temple
articles.summary: Nearly three weeks since two men were stabbed inside a Sikh temple in Edmonton, police have laid criminal charges in the case. Austin Sim-Pelletier, 27, has been charged with two counts of assault…

image.caption: Police in Edmonton have laid charges in the stabbing of two worshippers at a Sikh temple in the city's northeast on Aug. 21. (Sam Brooks/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·

Nearly three weeks since two men were stabbed inside a Sikh temple in Edmonton, police have laid criminal charges in the case. Austin Sim-Pelletier, 27, has been charged with two counts of assault causing bodily harm and two counts of possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose and mischief.
Accused was granted statutory release from federal prison day before attack
Live Edmonton police update on Sikh temple stabbing investigation
Nearly three weeks since two men were stabbed inside a Sikh temple in Edmonton, police have laid criminal charges in the case.

In a news release Thursday, police said Austin Sim-Pelletier, 27, has been charged with two counts of assault causing bodily harm, two counts of possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, and mischief.
Sim-Pelletier was charged on Sept. 4 and his next court appearance is scheduled for Friday, police said.
In Thursday's statement, police said they will continue to investigate a possible motive, including whether the attack was a hate crime.

“This investigation is complex and involves numerous investigative steps that we are still diligently working to complete,” Staff Sgt. Eric Stewart, with the EPS Investigations Branch, said in the statement.
Stewart is expected to speak at a news conference scheduled for 1 p.m. MT. Thursday. CBC News will carry the news conference live.
Police said the accused, who had been released from a federal prison outside the Edmonton region the day before, entered the Nanaksar Gurdwara on Aug. 21 during morning prayers.
Police said the man entered attempted to access the prayer area when he was confronted by staff.
The victims, aged 51 and 75, were taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries after the attacker was wrestled to the ground by temple attendees and arrested by patrol officers.

items: Stabbing at Edmonton Sikh temple leaves 2 injured, man in custody

blocks.text: The violent incident inside the sprawling temple on the northeastern outskirts of the city has prompted widespread condemnation from political leaders and Sikh community advocates and raised questions about the release of federal offenders who may pose a risk to public safety.
Sikh communities have documented a rise in recent discriminatory threats and attacks.
During a news conference last month, police said the suspect had a “significant” history of violent crime dating back more than a decade.
The accused had just served a sentence for aggravated assault and assault on a peace officer.
He had been held in custody these past weeks on a warrant issued for his failure to report to his designated Edmonton halfway house in the hours before the attack.
Statutory release 'not a choice'
In her statement condemning the attack last month, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said the stabbings should serve as a reminder of the need for federal bail and parole reform.

In a statement to CBC News on Aug. 24, the Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) stated that the suspect had been discharged from custody on statutory release — a policy which means federal officials have little leeway over his removal from custody.

“Statutory release is not a choice or discretionary decision by CSC — it is required by law after an offender serves two-thirds of a fixed-length federal sentence, with the offender being supervised in the community under conditional release,” the statement reads.
Statutory release requires the Correctional Service of Canada to release most federal prisoners into the community under supervision.

Unlike day and full parole, statutory release is not subject to decisions by the Parole Board of Canada but inmates released under the federal policy are required to report regularly to a parole officer and remain subject to conditions.
Most offenders qualify, with the exception of those serving a life sentence or an indeterminate sentence because of a dangerous offender designation issued by the court.
'Where the chain breaks down'

Michael Spratt, an Ottawa-based criminal defence lawyer with APG LLP, told CBC News last month that statutory release laws are "very, very effective" overall, but questioned systemic enforcement when breaches occur.
When an offender breaks release conditions — such as failing to report to a halfway house — infractions are reported quickly, Spratt noted.
He said public scrutiny should focus on how fast law enforcement responds to issue warrants and apprehend individuals in breach, he said.
“The public is rightly concerned when someone does offend on statutory release or on bail," Spratt said.
"We often focus on the tragedy of the offence, but we don't focus on the police response … quite often that's where the chain breaks down.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Wallis Snowdon is a journalist with CBC Edmonton focused on bringing stories to the website and the airwaves. Originally from New Brunswick, Wallis has reported in communities across Canada, from Halifax to Fort McMurray. She previously worked as a digital and current affairs producer with CBC Radio in Edmonton. Share your stories with Wallis at wallis.snowdon@cbc.ca.
With files from Brennan Klak

articles.title: ECB raises interest rates to fight off inflation jump
articles.summary: The European Central Bank raised borrowing costs and warned that inflation could remain high for an extended period. Energy markets and geopolitical tensions are still major concerns.

image.caption: Amid mounting inflationary pressures and a shaky energy market, the ECB has decided to tighten its policyImage: Jana Rodenbusch/REUTERS

blocks.text: The European Central Bank (ECB) raised interest rates on Thursday, hoping to curb rising inflation driven by higher energy costs stemming from the war between the US and Iran. This is the second increase that the ECB has had to implement this year. Risingoil and natural gas prices pushed inflation above 3% in the 21-country eurozone, surpassing the previous target of 2%.
"The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside of inflation and to the downside of economic growth," the ECB said in a statement after its annual meeting, held this year in Berlin.

The ECB also announced its economic growth projection for 2026. The study reveals slight growth of 0.9% compared to 0.8% in June, and inflation is now expected to average 3.0% this year and 2.5% in 2027.

Without a clear resolution to the US-Israel conflict with Iran, which began in late February, energy costs continue to rise, suggesting persistent inflation. There is also growing concern about gas storage levels, which remain below historical norms as the winter heating season approaches.
Why Iran fuel crisis hits different in Europe than the US
Economic outlook remains uncertain
"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," according to the ECB.

For countries in the eurozone, another hike in rates means more expensive mortgages, consumer credit, and loans. There has been little indication that eurozone inflation is being passed more broadly through the economy via higher prices for food, goods, or services.

Experts say the European Central Bank is worried about raising rates too slowly again. The last time it needed to take measures at this pace was in 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"The inflation outlook has worsened over the summer," said Sylvain Broyer, chief economist for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa at S&P. "Supply shocks are not only multiplying, but it is increasingly likely that demand is also contributing to inflation," he said.

articles.title: India-China thaw: 5 things to know as Xi heads to Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI, India — Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to India for a summit on Saturday that could mark the biggest step in a cautious thaw after years of hostility between the two countries.…

blocks.text: NEW DELHI, India — Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to India for a summit on Saturday that could mark the biggest step in a cautious thaw after years of hostility between the two countries.
Xi’s visit for the September 12-13 BRICS summit would be his first trip to India since October 2019 and follows Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s August 2025 visit to China.
The nuclear-armed Asian giants have been slowly improving ties since a deadly 2020 border clash. Flights, some visas and high-level contacts have gradually resumed.
But deep mistrust remains, with their disputed Himalayan frontier, a heavy trade deficit and strategic rivalry complicating ties.
Here are five things to know:
Border comes first
The relationship was transformed by the June 2020 Himalayan border clash, when fighting in Ladakh killed 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers.
In October 2024, Beijing and Delhi agreed on patrolling arrangements, paving the way for renewed political contacts.
But the underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometer (2,175-mile) high-altitude border along Tibet.
“They are looking for ‘early and substantial harvest’ when it comes to the border issue,” said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
“You cannot have a buildup of your forces on the border… but at the same time say ‘we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.'”
The Dalai Lama also lives in exile in India, ever since the Buddhist spiritual leader fled the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, after Chinese troops crushed an uprising in 1959.
Beijing condemns the Dalai Lama as a rebel and separatist.
Unequal trade ties
China is now India’s largest trading partner, with bilateral goods trade reaching $151 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, according to Indian government data.
But the relationship is heavily tilted toward Beijing.
India imported $131 billion of goods from China, while exports were $19 billion, leaving a record $112 billion trade deficit.
Modi’s government is pushing domestic manufacturing and seeking to reduce dependence on China for machinery, electronics, chemicals and industrial components.
But Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said India needs Chinese technology.
“India… need China’s — not just investment — but more and more technology,” he said.
China, he added, also wants to expand trade “even though India keeps complaining about the trade imbalance.”
Partners and rivals
Both are members of BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO).
Taneja argued that for Beijing, Xi’s “primary reason” for the visit is to bolster BRICS as an “alternative institution” to US-dominated institutions.
But they are also competitors.
India’s security partnership with Washington, including its participation in the so-called Quad security alliance with Japan and Australia, is viewed warily by Beijing.
China’s close relationship with India’s arch-rival Pakistan is viewed with concern by New Delhi.

“The very fact that President Xi is coming to India does indicate that… even if it’s because of the turbulence in the world caused by America, the two countries want a working relationship,” said Ashok Malik of The Asia Group.
Confidence-building measures
Ties have slowly warmed since 2024. That includes moves to revive border trade across their Himalayan frontier, ease visas and allow Indians to resume a key Hindu pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.
Direct flights, suspended for more than five years, resumed in October 2025.
“The relationship is now being put back on track,” said Harsh V. Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation.
“But it is more stabilization, rather than any dramatic change.”
Test, not breakthrough
Modi and Xi last held formal bilateral talks at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025.
Their brief interaction at this month’s SCO summit in Bishkek offered another public signal of a thaw.
But analysts remain cautious.

“The mistrust between India and China is so huge,” said Pant. “Unless there is a demonstrable shift in Chinese behavior, it is very unlikely that many in India would buy the India-China friends narrative.”

articles.title: China extends anti-dumping probe into pecans from US, Mexico
articles.summary: BEIJING, China — China has extended an anti-dumping investigation into pecans from the United States and Mexico, Beijing’s commerce ministry said on Thursday, two weeks before an expected visit…

blocks.text: BEIJING, China — China has extended an anti-dumping investigation into pecans from the United States and Mexico, Beijing’s commerce ministry said on Thursday, two weeks before an expected visit by President Xi Jinping to Washington.
The probe launched last year was originally expected to expire on September 25, one day after President Donald Trump’s anticipated meeting with Xi in the US capital.
The investigation has now been extended until March 25 next year, the Chinese commerce ministry said in a statement on Thursday, citing “the complexity of this case.”
Beijing began imposing steep levies of 54.3 percent on pecans from the United States and between 17.8 percent and 51.6 percent on those from Mexico in August.
The fees were initiated after the commerce ministry’s “preliminary ruling” found that pecans were being dumped in the Chinese market, “causing substantial damage to the relevant domestic industry.”
The United States and Mexico are the world’s biggest producers of pecans.
US exports of the nuts to China were worth $93.1 million in 2023, according to the US Foreign Agricultural Service.
The row over pecans adds to rumbling frictions in trade relations between the world’s top two economies, which escalated sharply last year following Trump’s return to the White House.

Beijing and Washington reached a shaky truce late last year in a tit-for-tat tariff war initiated by Trump, although China’s towering trade surplus and fierce technological competition still spur tensions.

articles.title: Are electric vehicles really bad for the environment?
articles.summary: Some German politicians are calling for a delay to the EU plan to phase out gas-powered vehicles, saying cars must be judged on the entire carbon footprint. But the full picture still says EVs are…

image.caption: The electricity used to charge EVs can contribute to carbon emissions, if it comes from burning fossil fuels like coal and gasImage: Gero Rueter/DW

blocks.text: "The EU's car lie" — Germany's Bild tabloid newspaper didn't mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union's "dangerous" claim that electric vehicles were carbon neutral.

Markus Söder, the conservative state premier of Bavaria — home to major automotive brands like Audi, BMWand Mercedes-Benz — was equally direct. Writing on social media, he called for an end to "the EU's phaseout of internal combustion engines" set for 2035. Such a policy shift, he said, was now backed by "science."

Söder and Bild were reacting to a new report by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), which outlined what it considered to be a major flaw in the EU's climate strategy: the fact that its vehicle emissions regulation only focuses on CO2 emissions from exhaust gases and that battery-electric vehicles are considered "climate-neutral."
EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure

The report stated that battery-electric vehicles reduce carbon emissions by only "41% on average" over combustion engine vehicles, with the EU regulation failing to take into account emissions generated by other factors like manufacturing and electricity mix.

Gas-powered vehicles were at a disadvantage, the report concluded, suggesting emissions should be counted over a vehicle's entire life cycle, from the materials used to build a car to the fuel that makes it run. Credit could be given for the use of green steel, for instance, or recovering raw materials through recycling.
It highlighted several major car manufacturers that support this approach, including BMW, Audi and Volkswagen — all major institutional donors at TUM.
No new insights in TUM report

Georg Bieker, who researches the environmental impact of electric and gas-powered cars at the US-based International Council on Clean Transportation think tank, said TUM's analysis didn't offer any new insights. He, and other climate and mobility experts, pointed out that the importance of life-cycle assessments was already well known.

Bieker co-authored a 2025 study examining the global warming potential of passenger cars sold in the EU which took into account their entire life cycle, from the production of the vehicle to its fuel consumption and maintenance. It found that the emissions generated by battery-electric vehicles are on average 73% lower than gasoline cars, and up to 78% when using only renewable electricity. Similar studies, including from the EU and the International Energy Agency, came up with emissions reductions of between 60%-66%. The Germany Environment Ministry said modern vehicles could even achieve reductions of up to 80%.

Hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, which combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery charged by the car's brakes and an internal generator, generate fewer emissions than traditional cars, but still don't match fully electric vehicles.

Bieker said the full EV advantage will only grow as production and operation becomes less carbon intensive. Even today, he added, production emissions for gasoline internal combustion vehicles only account for around 13% of the total climate impact; most of the emissions come from the tailpipe.
Batteries have a high environmental cost

Bieker confirmed batteries were still one of the main environmental challenges facing electric cars. The mining of key resources like cobalt and lithium has been linked to habitat destruction and water depletion; mining 1 ton of lithium, enough for around 125 EVs, requires some 2 million liters of water.

The ICCT study found that while battery-electric vehicles had an estimated 40% higher production emissions than gas-powered vehicles due to battery production, these additional emissions were offset after driving about 17,000 kilometers (10,500 miles), or in one or two years. And, Bieker pointed out, most of those batteries could eventually be recycled — unlike the gasoline burned in a combustion engine.

blocks.caption: While lithium-iron phosphate batteries tend to be cheaper and last longer, nickel manganese cobalt batteries deliver more power and work better in colder climatesImage: Rodrigo Freitas/NTB/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We see a trend of emissions decreasing for battery production," Bieker told DW, pointing out that technology was still being developed. The production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, for example, generates fewer emissions than the nickel manganese cobalt variety. LFPs are increasingly becoming the battery of choice for the industry — they're generally safer, last longer and are cheaper to manufacture.

Bieker said batteries were also increasingly being produced in Europe in larger, more efficient factories, which also helps reduce emissions generated by importing them from abroad. Though Europe still ranks second behind China when it comes to battery cell manufacturing, the European Commission has committed to boosting the sector with financial support, including a recent €1.5 billion in interest-free loans.
Czechia's lithium mine plans spark resistance
Renewable energy making the case for EVs

The other major factor contributing to EV emissions is the electricity mix — how the power charging the batteries is actually generated. While electric cars don't produce emissions during driving, they can generate them indirectly when charged using electricity produced by burning fossil fuels like coal and gas.
But the rapid expansion of renewable energy in recent years — especially solar, including a growing popularity of home installations — is increasingly tipping the scale in favor of EVs.

blocks.caption: Home solar power installations have taken off in Germany, giving EV owners a cheaper way to charge their carsImage: Daniel Reinhardt/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Europe's electricity grid is currently more than 70% decarbonised and expected to be almost fully decarbonised by 2040," said Gabrielle Clark, a policy officer at European trade federation Eurelectric focusing on energy, climate and sustainability. "As the production of green steel and battery recycling capacity also ramps up as expected, this will also only strengthen the case even more."

Clark said it wasn't necessary to replace the EU's current tailpipe emissions regulation, which plans to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035, with more complex regulations and green accounting rules.

"Whether assessed through [life-cycle assessment] or tailpipe emissions, [battery-electric vehicles] are always the preferred technology for carbon emission reductions in the road transport sector," she told DW in an email. "Their replacement of ICE vehicles must be accelerated, not delayed."
Rising fuel prices, climate concerns push EV growth
Bieker said that in the end the market will decide, not policy.

"The future will be electric, no matter what European policymakers or German carmakers think," he said, highlighting the global growth of EV sales in recent years, especially in China and Southeast Asia.

blocks.caption: EV sales have increased in Asia in recent years, with China's BYD leading the packImage: Andy Wong/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: EVs are also taking off in Europe. In Germany, for example, a new survey by research firm SBD Automotive and Here Technologies showed that 54% respondents were more likely to consider buying an electric car as their next vehicle, citing technology advances, rising fuel prices and environmental concerns.
"We cannot win the race by ignoring it," said Bieker. "[For climate,] for competitiveness and economic development, we need to double down on electrification and not slow it down."
Ethiopia's EV boom: A role model for all?

articles.title: Eight-gold target set as Philippines eyes Asian Games splash
articles.summary: Bannered by star athletes Carlos Yulo, Alex Eala, EJ Obiena, and Annie Ramirez, Team Philippines seeks to breach the four-gold mark in an Asian Games edition for the first time since 1962

blocks.text: EIGHT. Athletes, coaches, and officials during Team Philippines' send-off for the 2026 Asian Games and 2026 Asian Para Games.
Philippine Olympic Committee's Facebook page
Bannered by star athletes Carlos Yulo, Alex Eala, EJ Obiena, and Annie Ramirez, Team Philippines seeks to breach the four-gold mark in an Asian Games edition for the first time since 1962

items: Team Philippines aims to win at least eight gold medals at the upcoming Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, doubling their previous best of four golds.
To motivate the athletes, additional allowances and bonuses have been announced for exceeding past medal tallies, with the Asian Games set to begin on September 19.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Team Philippines has not won more than four gold medals in the Asian Games for over six decades, but the ambitious goal for the upcoming edition in Nagoya, Japan, is to win twice as many.

Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham “Bambol” Tolentino on Thursday, September 10, said the target for the quadrennial showpiece is at least eight gold medals, believing the 464-strong delegation can surpass the four-gold hauls each in 2018 in Indonesia and in 2023 in China.

“I’m not going to put any pressure on the athletes for this Asian Games. There will be no pressure, but give it everything you’ve got. Give it your absolute best,” said Tolentino in Filipino during the athletes’ send-off at the Rizal Memorial Coliseum.
The Philippines last breached the four-gold mark in the 1962 edition, where it clinched seven gold medals to finish fifth overall.
All but one of the Philippines’ four gold medalists in 2023 are still around, with Gilas Pilipinas, pole vault stalwart EJ Obiena, and jiu-jitsu standout Annie Ramirez aiming to defend their thrones.
Jiu-jitsu veteran Meggie Ochoa, another champion in 2023, has already retired from the national team and transitioned into coaching.
Aside from the three returning titleholders, gold medals are expected from gymnastics ace Carlos Yulo and tennis star Alex Eala.

Yulo, the Philippines’ first and only Olympic double gold medalist, bagged the floor exercise crown in the Asian Artistic Gymnastics Championships in June, while Eala has posted promising results, winning her first-ever WTA Tour title at the Washington Open in August, in between a fourth-round appearance in Wimbledon and a third-round stint in the US Open.
Other gold-medal prospects, according to Tolentino, come from boxing, taekwondo, wushu, mixed martial arts, athletics, esports, and skateboarding.
“There are no replays here. Give it everything you’ve got,” said Tolentino.
In a bid to motivate the delegates, Philippine Sports Commissioner chairman Patrick “Pato” Gregorio announced an additional P6,000 allowance for each participating athlete and coach.
Gregorio also promised bonuses if the country exceeds the four-gold Asian Games tally and 10-gold Asian Para Games yield in 2023.
“Let us achieve more, and when you come back, you will have a very good Christmas, I assure you,” said Gregorio. “Let us make the Filipino nation smile.”

The Asian Games will officially open on September 19 and run until October 4, but the men’s basketball tournament already started, with Gilas Pilipinas kicking off its title defense against Bahrain on Friday, September 11. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Japan seeks change to new UN world map over Russia ‘misconception’
articles.summary: TOKYO, Japan — Japan said on Thursday it had asked for the revision of a new world map adopted by the United Nations because it made the disputed Kuril Islands appear to belong to Russia. The UN…

blocks.text: TOKYO, Japan — Japan said on Thursday it had asked for the revision of a new world map adopted by the United Nations because it made the disputed Kuril Islands appear to belong to Russia.
The UN General Assembly voted on Friday to adopt the new map, which makes the African continent larger while also shrinking North America and Europe, drawing condemnation from the United States.
Japan was among the 164 UN members that supported the resolution but has now taken issue with it because it shows the Kurils, known in Japan as the Northern Territories, in the same color as Russia.
Top Japanese government spokesman Minoru Kihara said the new map, known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection, “contained a depiction contradicting the Japanese government’s position.”
“We lodged a protest with the map site’s operator through our diplomatic channel to demand the correction of this depiction,” Kihara told reporters.
He declined to say when the issue was brought to the government’s attention but said Japan “needs to prevent misconceptions of our territories and geographical names from spreading.”
The disputed islands were seized in 1945 by the former Soviet Union, which then expelled the Japanese population.
Relations between Japan and Russia soured significantly last month when President Vladimir Putin made a surprise visit to the disputed islands for the first time.
Japan swiftly summoned Moscow’s ambassador, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi saying Putin’s visit “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people” and calling it “absolutely unacceptable.”
She said the islands were “an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law.”
Moscow quickly hit back, saying it “categorically” rejects such statements, “which we consider politically inappropriate, insulting and, of course, legally unfounded.”
The UN said the new map aims to present “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses than was portrayed by more traditional Mercator projections.

articles.title: Death toll from cargo ship fire in China rises to 25
articles.summary: BEIJING, China — The death toll from a fire that erupted on Thursday on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked in a Chinese port has risen to 25, including five people who had been listed as missing,…

blocks.text: BEIJING, China — The death toll from a fire that erupted on Thursday on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked in a Chinese port has risen to 25, including five people who had been listed as missing, state media said.
The bulk carrier, moored in the eastern shipping hub of Qingdao, had 42 people on board when the fire broke out, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
Seventeen of those were evacuated, including five who were injured.
However, by Thursday evening, “all 25 missing persons had been found, none showing signs of life,” state broadcaster CCTV reported.
It said “the open flames were extinguished” by about 2:30 p.m. (0630 GMT).
State news agency Xinhua said earlier that the fire broke out at around 11:15 a.m. during the ship’s port call for maintenance, without specifying the cause of the fire.
A witness from a neighboring residential compound told AFP he saw thick smoke coming from the ship but did not hear an explosion.
“I saw the smoke from the ship by chance, but there was no visible fire,” he said.
“I didn’t hear an explosion or smell anything.”
The Xinhua state news agency shared video of the scene showing a large ship called the Ocean Melody docked at a yard, with dozens of rescuers swarming its decks and entering the vessel.
Several fire trucks and ambulances were stationed on the dock in front of the ship.
Ocean Melody is a 190-meter (623-foot) long bulk carrier sailing under the Liberian flag, according to the vessel-tracking website MarineTraffic, which located the ship as moored in Qingdao.
‘Profound lesson’
Qingdao is the hometown and namesake of Tsingtao beer and a major international maritime hub, connected to more than 700 ports in over 180 countries and regions, according to state media.
The Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding yard operates as a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation.
President Xi Jinping “stressed the need to… strictly hold those responsible to account,” Xinhua reported.
Xi said that “all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards.”
There have been several major industrial accidents in China over the past year, where safety regulations are often lax.
An explosion and ensuing fire at a shipyard in eastern Fujian province in August killed one fire and rescue worker and injured 12 others, according to state media.
China launched a campaign against fire hazards in high-rise buildings in November after a huge blaze engulfed several residential tower blocks in Hong Kong, killing 168 people.
A blast at a fireworks factory in central China killed 37 people in May, marking one of the nation’s deadliest industrial accidents in years.
And a fire in a shoe factory in Fujian in July killed at least 28 people.

articles.title: Get to know the Philippines’ 10 new national artists
articles.summary: Among the newly named national artists are four luminaries who are being conferred with the honor posthumously

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Every three years, a new set of Filipino individuals receive the country’s highest honors for their contributions to Philippine arts and all its forms. These pioneers are chosen and vetted by the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) and the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP), and later conferred by the president of the Philippines.

The last set of national artists were named in 2022 and included screenwriter and novelist Ricky Lee, dancer Agnes Locsin, stage director and theater actor Antonio “Tony” Mabesa, cartoonist Lauro “Larry” Alcala, poet Gemino Abad, fashion designer Salvacion Lim-Higgins, soprano Fides Cuyugan-Asensio, actress Nora Aunor, and director Marilou Diaz-Abaya.

This time, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. named 10 new national artists under Proclamation No. 1414 across the fields of literature, film and broadcast arts, visual arts, architecture, music, fashion design, and dance.
Get to know them and their legacies here.
Born and raised in Camiling, Tarlac, Gregorio Brillantes was a decorated author who was dubbed the “master of the Filipino short story” and “the godfather of Philippine speculative fiction.”

Brillantes stood as one of the most defining voices in Philippine fiction in English as we know it today. He published a vast array of influential works that cut across generations, such as The Distance to Andromeda and Other Stories; Faith, Love, Time, and Dr. Lazaro; and The Apollo Centennial.
He also wrote and edited for the publications Sunburst, The Manila Review, Focus, Asia-Philippines Leader, and the Philippines Free Press.

Brillantes received his BLitt degree, major in journalism, from Ateneo de Manila University in 1952. He racked up several accolades throughout his decades-long career, including being inducted into the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature Hall of Fame and receiving the Gawad CCP para sa Sining, among many other awards.
He died on September 26, 2025, at 92 years old.
Armando “Bing” Lao was a filmmaker, director, editor, and screenwriter regarded as a pillar in Philippine cinema.

He was the man behind the screenplays of the iconic films Takaw Tusko (1986), Itanong Mo sa Buwan (1988), Hati Tayo Sa Magdamag (1989), Fetch a Pail of Water (1999), La Vida Rosa (2001), and Biyaheng Lupa (2009), to name a few.

Lao was named New Wave Best Director and took home the title of New Wave Best Feature Film at the 2013 Manila Film Festival for his film, Dukit. He was also the recipient of one FAMAS award for Hati Tayo Sa Magdamag and five Gawad Urian awards for Takaw Tukso, Itanong Mo sa Buwan, Fetch a Pail of Water, Larger than Life, and La Vida Rosa, among other awards.
In 2024, he received the lifetime achievement award from the Film Development Council of the Philippines during its annual Parangal ng Sining, which recognizes luminaries in local cinema.
He passed away on June 18, 2024, at 75.
Born on April 9, 1915, in Manila, University of Santo Tomas alumnus Gabriel “Gabby” Formoso was a soft-spoken master builder who was regarded as the “Architect of a Modernizing Philippines.”
He was one of the first 100 architects of the Philippines. He was nominated for the National Artist honors as early as 2003.

Over 80 landmark buildings and 159 private homes bear his handprint, including the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Complex, the wood-accented Asian Institute of Management, The Manila Peninsula, and the historic Club Filipino clubhouse.
He graduated with an architecture degree from UST in 1937. Admired by the United Architects of the Philippines, he received the UAP Likha Award and Gold Medal.
He died at the age of 81 on December 22, 1996.
Born on May 15, 1938, in Silay City, Negros Occidental, Teodoro “Teddy” Hilado was a theater administrator who was dubbed the “Father of Lightning Design in Philippine Theater.”
Hilado served as the resident technical director for the CCP from 1969 to 1973, and a theater director of the Folks Arts Theater from 1973 to 1986.

He brought back to life hundreds of iconic dance, drama, and opera productions for organizations like Ballet Philippines and the Bayanihan Philippine National Folk Dance Company — where he met the love of his life, Rosky Balahadia. Their heartwarming, real-life romance at the CCP later became the soul behind the award-winning music video for the Itchyworms’ “Di Na Muli,” where Rosky returned to the CCP stage after over 20 years to dance once more under the spotlights designed in Teddy’s honor by his former protege, Shakira Villa-Symes.

blocks.caption: Get to know the Philippines’ 10 new national artists

blocks.text: Beyond traditional theater, he also designed ecosystem installations, including the Dr. Jose P. Rizal Light and Sound Presentation located at Rizal Park. He racked up several awards throughout his career, including being the first recipient of the Gawad CCP for Excellence in Lightning Design and Technical Theater in 1997, receiving the CCP Centennial Honors for the Arts in 1998.
Hilado died at the age of 77 on December 23, 2015.

Imelda Cajipe-Endaya is a Manila-based painter and printmaker known for her mixed media depictions of children, the environment, gender, empowerment, and Filipino identity, among many other disciplines. The 76-year-old is the first woman to be named national artist in the visual arts category.
She earned her bachelor’s degree in fine arts from University of the Philippines (UP) in 1970 and later completed her graduate studies in art history and criticism in 1975 and 1976, respectively.
In a video feature by Silverlens Galleries in 2025, Endaya confessed that she had long been labeled by writers as a feminist before she even knew what that concept was.
“I was simply painting about my own experience as a woman through the years,” she said.

To date, Endaya has received countless major awards for her work, such as the CCP’s Thirteen Artist Awards in 1990, the Araw ng Maynila Award in 1998, the CCP Centennial Honors for the Arts in 1999, and the NCCA’s Ani ng Dangal in 2009, to name a few.

Hailing from Sagay, Negros Occidental, Nunelucio “Nune” Alvarado is a 76-year-old painter whose works explore social realism. He paints through his battle with dementia through portraits of farm workers and vivid portrayals of community, political injustice, and struggle.
He is a progressive figure in the local art scene and the pride and joy of Negros Island, channeling his activism into spotlighting the marginalized sectors in his community through his paintings.

Alvarado was a recipient of the CCP’s Thirteen Artists Awards in 1992, and in 2004 received the Patnubay ng Sining at Kalinangan sa Larangan ng Pintura, a lifetime achievement award given by the same government agency.

blocks.caption: Sagay dedicates mural to dementia-stricken living art pillar

blocks.text: In May, Alvarado’s hometown Sagay put up a 30-meter-tall mural to honor his legacy as a living art pillar and continue to inspire the youth.

Born in 1928, Alfredo Buenaventura is a composer and conductor hailing from Santa Maria, Bulacan. He has composed over 1,000 works throughout his career, spanning operas, chamber music, symphonic poems, ballets, and many more. He has also composed numerous religious songs.
He was also an organist at the Manila Cathedral.
Some of his well-known masterpieces include “Lakambini,” “Mabuhay March,” “Bayan Kong Mahal,” “Dulambuhay,” and “Planting Rice.”
Buenaventura took up music at UST, the Centro Escolar University, and the Gregorian Institute. He served as the dean of CEU’s Conservatory of Music for 30 years.
Buenaventura received the Republican Cultural Heritage awards in 1964 for his composition of “Maria Makiling,” and in 1972 for his “Kayumanggi Symphony,” according to a Daily Tribune report.

Born in 1946 in Malolos, Bulacan, Nicanor Tiongson is a playwright, cultural scholar, and critic in the disciplines of history, literature, film, theater, popular culture, and art. He is professor emeritus at UP Film Institute and also served as dean of UP’s College of Mass Communication. As a cultural scholar, he was also the artistic director and vice president of the CCP.

In 1976, he co-founded the Manunuri ng Pelikulang Pilipino alongside Behn Cervantes, Nestor Torre, Petronilo Daroy, Pio de Castro III, Clodualdo del Mundo Jr., Justino Dormiendo, Mario Hernando, Bienvenido Lumbera, and Manny Pichel. This film circle is the award-giving body behind the Gawad Urian, which honors Filipino films and the people behind them.

Among his works, he wrote an impactful trilogy of essays on Philippine theater, which, as a whole, explores different art forms in theater, the evolution of local theater, and theater groups in the Philippines from the 1970s to the 1980s and the productions they mounted.

He wrote the historical book The Women of Malolos and Komedya sa Parañaque: Kasaysayan at Estetika, which tracks the growth of the comedy genre in San Dionisio and Don Galo in the city. The Ateneo de Manila University Press also published a compilation of Tiongson’s plays and musicals: Revitalizing Tradition and Resurrecting History.
In 2015, he won the Grand Goodman Prize for his “substantial contributions to Philippine historical studies.”

Born in Iloilo in 1950, Patis Tesoro initially dreamed of becoming a painter but would later be dubbed the “Grand Dame of Philippine Fashion” for her decades-long work reviving and reinventing Filipiniana.

Tesoro built her name by transforming indigenous Filipino textiles into barongs, kimono jackets, Maria Clara gowns, ternos, caftans, and richly embroidered tops, working piña, jusi, abaca, and cotton into pieces heavy with hand embroidery and indigenous patterns.

Her work has been staged in exhibitions and shows both locally and abroad, including “Piña: From Fabric to Couture” at the Hotel InterContinental Madrid in 2013, and “Kasuotang Filipino: Mga Likha ni Patis Tesoro” at the Museo ng Makati in 2023.

Tesoro pursued her education at Marygrove College in Detroit, Michigan, training to become an art educator before turning to fashion as a livelihood. Her revival of Filipiniana deepened through her collaboration with cultural advocate Ado Escudero on Katutubong Filipino, a project aimed at reviving the country’s dying traditional textiles.
Born on October 24, 1950, in Calbiga, Samar, Rafael “Nonoy” Froilan is one of the Philippines’ most celebrated male ballet dancers and has come to be known as the country’s premier danseur.
Froilan trained with the University of the East Dance Troupe before joining the CCP Dance School in 1972 and Ballet Philippines the following year.

For more than two decades, he served as principal dancer of Ballet Philippines, originating roles created specifically for him, including Norman Walker’s Songs of a Wayfarer and National Artist Alice Reyes’ Rama Hari and Carmina Burana. He also famously danced opposite Dame Margot Fonteyn and Yoko Morishita.
He has spent decades teaching at the Philippine High School for the Arts.
In 2020, he received the Gawad CCP Para sa Sining for Dance. – with reports from Arabella Grace Sta Ana and Jade Tan/Rappler.com
Arabella Grace Sta Ana is a Rappler intern studying BA Philosophy at UP Los Baños.
Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at UST Manila.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Why senators don’t need Senate clearance for personal trips
articles.summary: A Senate policy exempts senators, and Senate employees from seeking travel clearance for personal trips

blocks.text: IN SESSION. Senate President Win Gatchalian opens the second regular session of the 20th congress on July 27, 2026.
Angie de Silva/Rappler
A Senate policy exempts senators, and Senate employees from seeking travel clearance for personal trips

items: Senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Pia Cayetano have left the country amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte and budget deliberations.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said that senators do not need travel clearance for personal trips abroad, based on amended Senate rules.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Two more senators have left the country amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte and Senate deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.

On Thursday, September 10, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano and Senator Pia Cayetano had flown abroad, amid social media posts showing the senator-siblings allegedly arriving in Singapore on Wednesday evening, September 9.
A separate social media post also alleged that Taguig Mayor Lani Cayetano, Alan’s wife, flew to Singapore early Thursday.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he had yet to receive formal information about the Cayetano siblings’ departure but clarified that senators leaving the country for personal trips do not need to obtain travel clearance from the Senate.

blocks.caption: EXPLAINER: Why senators don’t need Senate clearance for personal trips

blocks.text: “I have yet to receive formal information if they left or not. The photos we are seeing on social media may be old pictures. However, senators leaving for abroad for personal reasons may do so without seeking clearance or notifying the Senate leadership,” Gatchalian said in a mix of English and Filipino.
Senator Loren Legarda, who remains on extended medical leave, also flew out of the country in August without seeking travel clearance.
Unlike official foreign trips, personal trips by senators do not require prior approval from the Senate president under current Senate rules.
Senate Policy Order No. 2016-003, approved by then-Senate president Franklin Drilon in July 2016, amended the Senate rules on official local and foreign travel.
The policy order struck out the provision stating that “all personal travels abroad of officials and personnel of the Senate shall be subject also to the approval of the Senate President.”
The amended provision instead states that official foreign travel by Senate members, officials and employees covered by the policy shall be subject to the prior approval of the Senate president.
“It was a personal trip and we don’t know the reason for it. We have no policy they need to seek permission for personal trips,” Gatchalian said.

“They need travel clearance for official trips, especially if the Senate needs to cover some of their expenses such as hotels, tickets, and staff allowance. Senators and employees need travel clearance when traveling on official notice,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Malta warned of corruption crisis after Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict sends ‘chill down the spine’
articles.summary: Labour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at risk

blocks.text: Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia.

Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017.
Malta is in turmoil after the acquittal of a wealthy and politically influential businessman, Yorgen Fenech, of any involvement in Caruana Galizia’s murder.
Fenech denies paying a middleman €150,000 to have her killed.
At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond.

blocks.caption: Shami Chakrabarti: ‘atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision’. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA

blocks.text: “It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.

The first witnesses on Wednesday were the journalist’s eldest son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, and her sister Corinne Vella, who questioned the verdict, which dismissed both charges against Fenech by an 8-1 majority.

Matthew Caruana Galizia told members of the council’s committee on legal affairs and human rights: “The Maltese public have seen all of the evidence against the accused, and the vast majority were convinced of his complicity in the murder. And this is why there is this atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision.”
Malta’s state prosecutor is understood to be preparing an appeal, with the aim of securing a retrial.

The Council for Europe, founded in 1949 after the second world war, created the European convention on human rights. It is led by an assembly drawn from members of the parliaments of its 46 member states.

During the hearing, representatives expressed shock and concern about the verdict, calling for the European parliament and the European Commission to intervene. Iulian Bulai, a Romanian centre-right politician, suggested the EU could withhold funds from Malta. The procedure, known as the rule of law conditionality mechanism, was first used in 2022, against Hungary.

“If there is such huge problem in matter of rule of law and a function of the Maltese institutions, the EU should apply a similar procedure on increasing pressure for reform,” said Bulai. He said the procedure had “functioned in other cases … So why shouldn’t it function in Malta’s case?”

blocks.caption: Daphne Caruana Galizia pictured in 2011. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters

blocks.text: Malta, the EU’s smallest member state, with a population of 600,000, is a net recipient of EU money. Analysis suggests that since joining the block 22 years ago, the island has received €2.4bn more in subsidies than it has paid in.
Chakrabarti said she would look at why Malta had failed to implement many of the recommendations from a public inquiry held after the murder.

“The targeted assassination of a journalist in the middle of investigating high level corruption sent a chill down the spine of everyone who cares about democratic values,” she said. “Many claim that the legal and policy changes needed to protect journalists to combat corruption and ensure the independent functioning of justice have not been carried out.

“I’m extremely concerned by the apparent absence of reforms in critical areas which make Malta vulnerable to repeated instances of high-level corruption and limit the press freedom which should hold it in check.”

blocks.caption: Yorgen Fenech leaving the courthouse in Valetta on 2 September after his acquittal.   Photograph: Kevin Schembri Orland/AP

blocks.text: The public inquiry found although there had been no evidence that the Maltese state had a direct role in the murder, the state bore responsibility for creating a climate of impunity.
It recommended Italian-style anti-mafia laws, and making the hindrance of police investigations and abuse of office a crime for public officials. These measures have yet to be implemented.

Chakrabarti compared the Caruana Galizia case to miscarriages of justice in the UK, where officials had been involved in coverups, citing the mismanagement of Grenfell Tower, the Post Office scandal and the Hillsborough football stadium disaster. She said her inquiry, titled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case, was likely to conclude in a year.

Vella said fear that serious crimes could go unpunished had increased since the verdict. “Before the verdict was given, we lived in a country where a journalist was killed, but there was a chance of ending impunity. That disappeared as soon as the verdict was out.”
She said journalists who have continued to investigate corruption allegations involving former members of Malta’s government “felt uneasy walking to their own cars following that verdict”.

articles.title: Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
articles.summary: Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has been on a diplomatic offensive since becoming president in April, but foreign friends may still be few and far between.

image.caption: As Myanmar's newly minted head of state, Min Aung Hlaing has been hosted by the leaders of India, China, Laos, Thailand, Russia and now Vietnam — six countries in five monthsImage: Aung Shine Oo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a three-day state visit on Sunday to Vietnam, where the Southeast Asian neighbors vowed to boost defense and security ties.

There was nothing unusual about the trip itself, except that it marked the ex-general's sixth official trip abroad since assuming Myanmar's presidency in April, when he was voted in by a parliament stacked with loyalists following military-run elections in December and January that were widely considered a charade.

As Myanmar's newly minted head of state, Min Aung Hlaing has been hosted by the leaders of India, China, Laos, Thailand, Russia and now Vietnam — six countries in five months. He'll be heading to Cambodia on Friday to make it seven.

"Since the December-January elections and Min Aung Hlaing's transition to president after giving up his role as commander-in-chief, he's really put a renewed focus on diplomatic partnership and trying to shore up the government's allies in the region,” said Hunter Marston, head of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank.

"Even if they're relatively short trips to regional friends and allies, I think it shows that there is an acceleration of Naypyitaw's strategy to diversify its partnerships and to normalize relations bilaterally,” he added, referring to Myanmar's capital.
Aung San Suu Kyi's son on the latest images of his mother
Human rights situation in Myanmar sinks to new low

Marston and other analysts told DW that Myanmar is slowly returning to the international stage, aiming to shed its pariah status despite the mountain of war crimes allegations leveled against the regime — some against Min Aung Hlaing himself.
Since Min Aung Hlaing's military toppled the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021, civil war has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million.

Last month, the United Nations said human rights conditions in the country had sunk to a new low, as the military keeps up a campaign of forced recruitment, arson and often indiscriminate air strikes on contested and resistance-held areas.

That record has also made Myanmar one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world and brought on a number of court filings for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity at The Hague and elsewhere.

Despite that record, "the military regime is emerging to some extent from its isolation, but engagement is still largely limited to countries that were working with it to some extent prior to the recent sham elections," said Scot Marciel, a senior adviser at the consulting firm BowerGroupAsia.

"The military clearly hopes increased engagement will give it legitimacy that will help it cement its status, but it has not gained any legitimacy among the Myanmar public," Marciel, a former US ambassador to Myanmar, added.
Rohingya caught in the middle of Myanmar's civil war
Divisions in ASEAN over Myanmar
Even among its Southeast Asian neighbors, holdouts remain.

Since the coup, the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which Myanmar is one, has barred Min Aung Hlaing and his foreign ministers from attending the bloc's most senior-level meetings.

Malaysia, Indonesia and current ASEAN chair, the Philippines, are especially adamant that it stay that way until Myanmar makes meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that all the members agreed to in April 2021.

Myanmar's regime has made little progress on the plan so far and rejected repeated requests for ASEAN's special envoys to the country to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi, who was arrested the morning of the coup and has been held in custody since.
Last month, the country's newly installed parliament passed a motion flatly rejecting the bloc's peace plan, and its Foreign Ministry said ASEAN's special envoys were no longer needed.

Under the circumstances, Min Aung Hlaing and his ministers are unlikely to be attending ASEAN's senior leaders summits "any time soon,” said Pinitbhand Paribatra, an associate professor of international relations at Thailand's Thammasat University.
Marston and Marciel, though, say there's a good chance ASEAN will welcome Myanmar fully back into the fold once Thailand assumes the bloc's rotating, one-year chairmanship in 2028.

With significant business and security interests in Myanmar and a shared border stretching over 2,400 kilometers, Thailand has been keen to placate the country's regime and to urge the rest of ASEAN to do the same.

Thailand's premier and foreign minister "have been very clear that they want to pursue calibrated engagement [with Myanmar] and that they have already seen sufficient progress to incentivize further engagement," said Marston.
New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugees
Japan willing to restore normal ties?

Beyond China, Russia and Southeast Asia, Marston and Pinitbhand say Myanmar may also find countries to reengage with among Russia's authoritarian allies in Central Asia and elsewhere. Min Aung Hlaing made visits to Belarus even before he was president.
Among democratic countries, Pinitbhand said Japan was "more than ready" to restore normal relations with Myanmar.

"I don't think that Min Aung Hlaing will be traveling to Japan any time soon. But … there might be some other attempts from Japan to, for example, resume the relationship, because the Japanese private sector already has lots of investments and everything inside the country," he said.
Marciel pointed to both Japan and South Korea as countries that might start normalizing their relations with Myanmar in the next year or so.

blocks.caption: The civil war in Myanmar has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million since 2021 [FILE: August 10, 2024]Image: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Will the West reengage with Myanmar?

As for countries in the West, the analysts say they see little to no chance of them welcoming Min Aung Hlaing and his regime back onto the world stage or of lifting the heavy sanctions they have placed on them.

Pinitbhand says that's especially true if the International Criminal Court ultimately decides to issue the arrest warrant its former chief prosecutor had asked for against Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity. A decision is still pending.

Marston says it's possible Washington would go for "calibrated reengagement" with Naypyitaw if it were to release Aung San Suu Kyi and follow up with other reforms, as the administration of former US President Barack Obama did when she was freed from house arrest in 2010.

"But in this case, I don't think there are the leader-level engagements to begin to have that conversation between Naypyitaw and Washington, or the strategic interest within the Trump administration to do so," he said.

Marciel also said that Myanmar was low on the Trump administration's list of priorities. But with human rights also low on that list, he added, there was a chance it would warm to the regime for the right commercial or economic opportunities.
On the whole, though, the former ambassador says the West won't be embracing Min Aung Hlaing and his regime for now.

"I don't see any movement to ease sanctions among the Western countries that maintain them, as they all see the recent elections as a sham and also do not give much priority to Myanmar matters in their foreign policy," he said. "Things could change, but that is how it looks for now."

articles.title: Interviewer asks to be excused as witness in Marcoleta plunder trial
articles.summary: A broadcaster who interviewed Sen.Rodante Marcoleta has asked the Sandiganbayan to be excused as a witness in the plunder charge lodged against the lawmaker and three others.

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 8:07pm

A broadcaster who interviewed Senator Rodante Marcoleta has asked the Sandiganbayan to be excused as a witness in the plunder charge lodged against the Senator and three others over P75 million in alleged undeclared campaign donations.

Nelson Lubao, who interviewed Marcoleta during a November 8, 2025 television episode on Net 25, made the pleading in a manifestation with motion to be excused as witness for the prosecution, which he sent to the court via email on September 9, 2026.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division subpoenaed Lubao to testify in the case filed by government prosecutors against Marcoleta and his three campaign donors Joseph Varias Espiritu, Aristotle Baluyut Viray, and former Anakalusugan lawmaker Michael "Mike" Defensor.

The court’s subpoena stemmed from the motion made by the state prosecutors, given that it was Lubao who asked Marcoleta to explain why he declared a P52-million net worth in his SALN, way lower than his declared Statement of Campaign Expenditures at P139.9 million.
Lubao asked, “Ang sabi nila ay papaano nagkaroon ng expenditure na ganito kataas gayong ang kanyang asset ay mas maliit. Sen, papaano ba ang mga nangyari?”
(People are asking how the expenditures are this high for someone who has smaller assets? Kindly explain it, Senator.)
Marcoleta replied that he did not list his friends’ campaign contribution because they requested that their identities not be disclosed.

“Kapag naglagay ako ng figure sa contribution, mapipilitan ako mag-disclose ng pangalan nila dahil mayroon kaakibat na kung tawagin ay deed of acceptance of donation. Papaano iyon? Sabi niya, binigay ko nga sa iyo ‘yan. Ituring mo na lang na utang. Dahil sa hindi ko pwedeng isiwalat ang kanilang identity, kaya sinabi ko, zero in contribution,” he added.

(If I put a figure on their contribution, I would be forced to drop their names due to deed of acceptance of donation. How do I deal with it then? I was told that the money given to me can be treated as a loan. And since I cannot disclose their identity, I stated zero contribution.)
The Sandiganbayan Third Division gave both the prosecution and the defense 10 days to file their respective comment on Lubao’s motion to be excused.
Ombudsman prosecutors are alleging that Marcoleta unjustly enriched himself by accepting the P75 million gift from his co-accused in the case.

In addition, state prosecutors said that the donor’s tax for three tranches of the contribution given to Marcoleta by his co-accused in January 2025 were paid only in December 2025 which is in violation of Section 103(B) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, which provides: ‘The return of the donor required in this Section shall be filed within 30 days after the date the gift is made and the tax due thereon shall be paid at the time of filing.”
Also on Thursday, Marcoleta’s camp refused to stipulate, meaning agree, that the YouTube link of Lubao's November 8, 2025 interview with Marcoleta is genuine.

Marcoleta has denied liability in the plunder charge and views it as politically motivated amid his criticisms of the administration’s efforts to prosecute those involved in the flood control kickback scheme. — BM, GMA News

articles.summary: Facing 14 fatalities and more than 1,700 active dengue cases, Albay has mobilized its quick response fund to secure additional emergency medical kits and contain the outbreak

blocks.text: CROWDED HOSPITALS. Albay Governor Noel Rosal visits the Josefina Belmonte Duran Albay Provincial Hospital in Ligao City on September 9, 2026, where at least 100 dengue patients are currently confined.
Albay Governor Noel Rosal’s Facebook page.
Facing 14 fatalities and more than 1,700 active dengue cases, Albay has mobilized its quick response fund to secure additional emergency medical kits and contain the outbreak

items: The Provincial Government of Albay declared a state of calamity due to 1,785 dengue cases and 14 fatalities as of September 10.
Legazpi City has the highest number of active cases, prompting the government to mobilize emergency response efforts and implement containment measures.
Governor Noel Rosal emphasized the need for community participation in sanitation efforts to prevent further dengue transmission.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
ALBAY, Philippines – The Provincial Government of Albay declared a state of calamity after recording 1,785 dengue cases and 14 fatalities as of Thursday, September 10.

According to data from the Albay Provincial Health Office (PHO), Legazpi City logged the highest number of active cases at 378, with five fatalities, followed by Bacacay town with 254 active cases, and Daraga with 188 active cases and two fatalities. Active cases are currently being monitored across 15 other municipalities.

The declaration allows the provincial government to mobilize emergency response efforts, implement immediate containment measures, and access quick response funds to procure critical medical supplies and testing kits.
Albay Governor Noel Rosal said the declaration was deemed necessary as dengue cases continued to surge. He issued the declaration recommendation a day earlier, Wednesday, September 9.

“We are already beyond the epidemic level compared to the last three years, according to the Department of Health Region V,” Rosal said. “Let us continue the barangay brigades and clean our respective areas.”
Rosal had earlier issued Executive Order No. 51 on September 2, mandating sustained and community-based dengue prevention and control measures.

“The province shall strengthen the Albay Aksyon Barangay Kontra Dengue as a mechanism for mobilization, source reduction, health education, early identification of public health concerns, reporting, referral, and coordination with appropriate health authorities,” the order stated.
The Albay PHO urged residents to actively participate in community sanitation to halt transmission.

“The continuous increase in cases is a clear call for more intensified, sustained, and collective action to prevent further illness and loss of life,” the PHO stated. “Let us not wait for another case to emerge or another life to be lost before taking action. Every area we clean and every mosquito breeding site we eliminate is a step toward stopping dengue and saving lives.”
This marks the province’s first dengue-related state of calamity since 2019, when a similar declaration was issued alongside a national epidemic alert. – Rappler.com
